特性インピーダンス.desc: The ratio of voltage to current of a wave traveling in one direction on a transmission line. For a lossless line Z0 = √(L/C); it is set by the line's cross-sectional shape and materials and does not depend on its length.

about.h: Why a line has an impedance
about.p: At high frequencies, a signal on a wire is treated as a wave in which voltage and current travel together. A line has an inductance L per unit length and a capacitance C between its conductors, and as the wave advances it drives current into the L ahead of it and charges the C. As a result, the ratio of voltage to current that the source sees at the wavefront is constant, and this is the characteristic impedance Z0 = √(L/C). The key point is that, unlike a resistance that turns power into heat, it is the ratio of voltage to current while power is carried forward, and on a lossless line it has the same value regardless of length.

Z0 is set only by the cross-sectional dimensions of the line and the relative permittivity of the surrounding dielectric. For a coaxial line, Z0 = (60/√εr) ln(D/d) Ω; it rises as the ratio of the outer conductor's inner diameter D to the inner conductor's outer diameter d increases, and falls when a dielectric is added. For a microstrip line on a printed circuit board, Z0 is lower for a wider trace, a thinner substrate and a higher relative permittivity. In design, the trace width and layer stack are calculated to give the chosen Z0, and controlled with manufacturing tolerances in mind.

RF instruments and radios mostly use 50 Ω as the standard characteristic impedance. For an air-filled coaxial line, power handling is greatest at about 30 Ω and loss is lowest at about 77 Ω, and 50 Ω is often explained as a compromise between the two. Where little power is carried and low loss matters, as in TV and CATV receiving systems, 75 Ω is used. If Z0 is not uniform throughout a system, reflections occur at the boundaries, so a matching network is inserted when different systems are connected.

faq.q: Can characteristic impedance be measured with a multimeter?
faq.a: No. Characteristic impedance is the voltage-to-current ratio of a traveling wave, not a DC resistance. It is found by looking at the size of reflections with TDR, or by measuring the input impedance with the far end shorted and open on a network analyzer and computing √(Zshort·Zopen).

faq.q: Does making a line longer change its characteristic impedance?
faq.a: No. Z0 is set by the cross-sectional shape and materials. What changes with length is the input impedance when a mismatched load is connected.

faq.q: When do I need to worry about characteristic impedance?
faq.a: When the length of the wiring cannot be ignored compared with the wavelength, or, for digital signals, when the propagation delay cannot be ignored compared with the rise time. In those cases, if the load and Z0 do not match, reflections occur and the waveform is distorted.

反射係数.desc: The ratio of the voltage of the wave reflected at a load to that of the incident wave. Γ = (ZL − Z0)/(ZL + Z0); it is 0 for a match, −1 for a short and +1 for an open.

about.p: When a load ZL different from the characteristic impedance Z0 terminates a transmission line, part of the incident wave is reflected back. The ratio of the reflected to the incident voltage is the reflection coefficient, Γ = (ZL − Z0)/(ZL + Z0). If ZL = Z0 it is 0 and there is no reflection; a short (ZL = 0) gives −1 and an open (ZL = ∞) gives +1, both total reflection. If the load is complex, Γ is complex too; its magnitude gives the strength of the reflection and its phase the shift of the reflected wave. For a passive load, |Γ| does not exceed 1.

about.h: Relation to VSWR, return loss and mismatch loss
about.p: The size of a reflection is expressed in various forms depending on the purpose. The ratio of maximum to minimum voltage on the line is VSWR = (1 + |Γ|)/(1 − |Γ|); the ratio of reflected power in dB is the return loss RL = −20 log₁₀|Γ|; and the part that fails to reach the load because of reflection is the mismatch loss −10 log₁₀(1 − |Γ|²). For example, with |Γ| = 0.2, the VSWR is 1.5, the return loss about 14 dB, the reflected power 4%, and the mismatch loss about 0.18 dB. All of these describe the same amount of reflection, so they can be converted into one another.

about.h: Position-dependent reflection coefficient and the Smith chart
about.p: On a lossless line, the reflection coefficient at a point a distance l back from the load toward the generator is Γ(l) = ΓL·e^(−j2βl): its magnitude stays the same and only its phase rotates. Since β = 2π/λ, it makes one full turn every λ/2. Plotting this Γ on the complex plane and overlaying impedance scales gives the Smith chart, on which changes with line length appear as rotation around the center. On a network analyzer, the reflection coefficient is measured directly as S11.

faq.q: When is the reflection coefficient negative?
faq.a: When the load is a pure resistance smaller than the characteristic impedance. For example, terminating a Z0 = 50 Ω line in 25 Ω gives Γ = −1/3, and the reflected wave at the load points in the opposite direction to the incident wave.

faq.q: Are the reflection coefficient and S11 the same thing?
faq.a: For a two-port with port 2 terminated in a matched load, the reflection coefficient seen at port 1 is S11. For a one-port load (such as an antenna), S11 is that load's reflection coefficient itself.

faq.q: Can the reflection coefficient exceed 1?
faq.a: Not for a passive load. In active circuits with negative resistance (such as those used in oscillators), |Γ| > 1, and more power comes back than went in.

VSWR.desc: Voltage standing wave ratio: the ratio of maximum to minimum voltage on a line, VSWR = (1 + |Γ|)/(1 − |Γ|). It is 1 for a match and grows as the reflection increases.

about.p: When reflection occurs at the end of a line, the incident and reflected waves travel in opposite directions on the same line and interfere to form a standing wave. Where their phases align, the voltage amplitude reaches its maximum, V(1 + |Γ|), and where they are opposite it reaches its minimum, V(1 − |Γ|). The ratio of maximum to minimum is the voltage standing wave ratio (VSWR), VSWR = (1 + |Γ|)/(1 − |Γ|). Maxima and minima alternate every λ/4. In the past, a probe was moved along a slotted line to measure the voltage maxima and minima directly, revealing how well the load was matched.

A VSWR of 1 means a match, and infinity means total reflection. A VSWR of 1.5 corresponds to |Γ| = 0.2 with 4% of the power reflected; 2.0 to |Γ| = 1/3, about 11%; and 3.0 to 0.5, 25%. In terms of reflected power, even at a VSWR of 2 about 89% of the power reaches the load, a loss of only about 0.5 dB. Even so, antenna and transmitter specifications often set an upper limit on VSWR within the band, because reflections change how power amplifiers operate and alter circuit characteristics.

VSWR expresses only the magnitude of the reflection coefficient and carries no phase information, so designing a matching network also requires the impedance (or the phase of Γ). Also, if a lossy cable sits between the transmitter and the antenna, the reflected wave is attenuated on the round trip, so the VSWR measured at the transmitter looks better than the true VSWR at the antenna. For example, with 3 dB of one-way loss, even if the antenna reflects totally, the reflected wave weakens by 6 dB (1/4 in power) on the round trip, so |Γ| at the transmitter is about 0.5 and the VSWR appears to be about 3.

faq.q: How do I convert between VSWR and return loss?
faq.a: Convert to the reflection coefficient with |Γ| = (VSWR − 1)/(VSWR + 1), then take return loss = −20 log₁₀|Γ|. For a VSWR of 1.5, |Γ| = 0.2 and the return loss is about 14 dB.

faq.q: What problems does a high VSWR cause?
faq.a: Besides reducing the power reaching the load, in a transmitter the reflected power returns to the amplifier and causes distortion, heating and, in the worst case, damage to the devices. That is why protection circuits reduce the output, or isolators are inserted.

faq.q: Can the VSWR be less than 1?
faq.a: No. It is the ratio of the maximum to the minimum, so by definition it is always 1 or more.

リターンロス.desc: The ratio of reflected power to incident power expressed in dB. RL = −20 log₁₀|Γ|; the larger the value, the better the match.

λ/4変成器.desc: A matching network that transforms impedance with a line λ/4 long. Making its characteristic impedance √(Z0·ZL) matches ZL to Z0.

スタブ.desc: A short length of line with its far end shorted or open. Depending on its length it acts as an inductor or a capacitor, and it is used in matching networks and filters.

速度係数.desc: The ratio of the speed of propagation on a line to the speed of light. It is set by the relative permittivity εr of the dielectric as 1/√εr, and the wavelength on the line is shorter by this ratio.

スミスチャート.desc: A chart of normalized impedance drawn on the reflection-coefficient plane. It lets you treat transformation by lines and the design of matching networks as movement on circles.

about.p: The Smith chart overlays scales of normalized impedance z = Z/Z0 on the complex plane of the reflection coefficient Γ (a circle of radius 1). The center is z = 1 (a match), the left edge is a short (z = 0), the right edge is an open (z = ∞), the upper half is inductive and the lower half capacitive. Points of constant resistance r lie on circles tangent at the right edge (constant-resistance circles), and points of constant reactance x lie on arcs leaving the right edge. Its strength is that it fits the infinite impedance plane inside a circle and lets you read the reflection coefficient and impedance at the same time.

On a lossless line the magnitude of the reflection coefficient is constant and only its phase changes. So as line length is added from the load toward the generator, the point travels clockwise on a circle around the center of the chart (the constant-VSWR circle), making one full turn every λ/2. Half a turn at λ/4 moves z to 1/z, which also explains how a quarter-wave transformer works. The radius of the circle corresponds to the VSWR: the normalized resistance where the circle crosses the real axis to the right of the center equals the VSWR. On a lossy line, the point spirals gradually toward the center as it rotates.

Adding an inductor in series with a load leaves the resistance unchanged and increases only the reactance, so the point moves clockwise along a constant-resistance circle into the upper half; a series capacitor moves it counterclockwise into the lower half. Shunt elements move the point along constant-conductance circles of the admittance chart (the impedance chart rotated by 180°). An L-network can be designed as a path combining these movements to carry the load point to the center. Component values are read from the reactance or susceptance scale covered by each movement.

faq.q: What does the center of the Smith chart represent?
faq.a: A normalized impedance z = 1, meaning the load equals the characteristic impedance and there is no reflection. In matching network design, the goal is to bring the point to this center.

faq.q: How do I switch from impedance to admittance?
faq.a: The point rotated 180° about the center of the chart gives the normalized admittance y = 1/z. For example, rotating the point z = 1 + j1 gives y = 0.5 − j0.5.

faq.q: Is the Smith chart still used today?
faq.a: Yes. Drawing by hand has become less common, but it is widely used as a display in network analyzers and circuit simulators to see impedance changes intuitively.

Sパラメータ.desc: A way of describing a circuit by the ratios of the waves entering and leaving each port. S11 represents input reflection and S21 transmission, and they can be measured with matched terminations.

about.h: Describing a circuit by incident and reflected waves
about.p: S-parameters (scattering parameters) describe a circuit by the relationship between the waves a entering and b leaving each port. For a two-port, b1 = S11·a1 + S12·a2 and b2 = S21·a1 + S22·a2. S11 and S22 are the reflection coefficients of each port, S21 is forward transmission (the gain of an amplifier or the transmission of a filter), and S12 is reverse transmission (isolation). Each S-parameter is defined with the other ports terminated in the reference impedance. At high frequencies, ideal shorts and opens are hard to make, and active devices may oscillate when shorted or opened, so S-parameters, which can be measured with matched terminations, have become the standard.

S-parameters are complex numbers with magnitude and phase. They are ratios of wave amplitudes, so their magnitude in dB uses 20 log₁₀|S|; for example, |S21| = 0.5 is about −6 dB, and |S11| = 0.1 is a return loss of 20 dB. The phase carries electrical-length information, and differentiating the phase of S21 with respect to frequency gives the group delay. When evaluating a filter, the flatness of S21 in the passband, the attenuation in the stopband and S11 (reflection) in the passband are examined together.

Circuits containing no magnetic materials or active devices, such as resistors, L, C and lines, are reciprocal, and S21 = S12. In a lossless circuit power is conserved, so the S-matrix is unitary; for a two-port, |S11|² + |S21|² = 1. These relations let you check whether measured data are physically sound (for example, that the sum of transmission and reflection of a passive circuit does not exceed 1). Circulators and isolators using ferrite, and transistor amplifiers, are nonreciprocal, with S21 ≠ S12.

S-parameters are measured with a vector network analyzer (VNA). A VNA separates incident and reflected waves with directional couplers, but its measurements include errors from cable and connector loss and from insufficient coupler directivity, so it is calibrated before measuring. In the common SOLT calibration, a short, an open, a matched load and a thru are measured at the reference plane, and an error model is determined and removed. Measured data are typically saved in Touchstone format (.s2p and so on) and used in circuit simulators.

faq.q: What is the difference between S21 and S12?
faq.a: S21 is transmission from port 1 to port 2, and S12 is transmission from port 2 to port 1. In a passive reciprocal circuit they are equal; in an amplifier, S21 is the gain and S12 the reverse isolation.

faq.q: What impedance are S-parameters referenced to?
faq.a: The reference impedance chosen for the measurement or design, usually 50 Ω. Changing the reference impedance changes the S-parameter values, so the reference should always be stated with the data.

faq.q: Can cascaded circuits be calculated by multiplying S-parameters?
faq.a: Not directly. Convert them to T-matrices or ABCD matrices, multiply those, and convert back to S-parameters at the end.

挿入損失.desc: The fraction of power lost by inserting a component into the signal path, expressed in dB. In a matched system it is −20 log₁₀|S21|.

アイソレーション.desc: The attenuation between ports that ideally should not be connected, such as between the outputs of a divider or the reverse leakage of a circulator, expressed in dB.

方向性結合器.desc: A passive component that extracts part of a wave traveling on the main line while distinguishing its direction of travel. Its performance is described by coupling and directivity, and it is used to measure power and reflection.

ウィルキンソン分配器.desc: A power divider made from two λ/4 lines and a resistor between the outputs. Its input and outputs are matched, and high isolation is obtained between the output ports.

サーキュレータ.desc: A nonreciprocal device using ferrite that passes signals in only one direction, port 1 → 2 → 3. Terminating one port turns it into an isolator.

熱雑音.desc: Noise produced by the thermal motion of electrons in a resistance. Its power is kTB, proportional to bandwidth, and at 290 K it is −174 dBm per hertz.

雑音指数.desc: A value (NF), in dB, expressing how much a circuit degrades the SNR of a signal passing through it. It is defined with the input noise taken as thermal noise at 290 K.

about.p: Noise figure (NF) expresses how much the SNR worsens as a signal passes through a circuit. The noise factor F = (S/N)in/(S/N)out is defined with the input noise taken as thermal noise at the reference temperature T0 = 290 K, and NF = 10 log₁₀ F [dB]. An ideal circuit that adds no noise has F = 1 (0 dB). It is related to the equivalent noise temperature Te by Te = (F − 1)·T0; an NF of 1 dB corresponds to about 75 K and 3 dB to about 290 K. In the region below 1 dB, as for low-noise amplifiers, comparisons are often made in noise temperature, where differences are easier to see.

about.h: Multistage circuits and the Friis formula
about.p: The overall noise factor of a multistage circuit is found with the Friis formula F = F1 + (F2 − 1)/G1 + (F3 − 1)/(G1G2) + …. The noise of the second and later stages is divided by the gain of the stages before them, so the first stage's noise figure largely sets the total, and the larger the first-stage gain, the smaller the effect of later stages. For example, even with a 12 dB noise figure mixer after an LNA with 20 dB gain and a 2 dB NF, the total is about 2.4 dB. The calculation is done with linear values, not dB.

about.h: Loss in passive components and noise figure
about.p: A matched passive attenuator or line has a noise figure equal to its loss when the ambient temperature is 290 K. So the loss of cables and filters between the antenna and the LNA adds almost directly to the receiver's overall noise figure. In receivers needing high sensitivity, the LNA is placed close to the antenna and the loss of the front-end filter is kept small. Receiver sensitivity can be estimated as thermal noise of −174 dBm/Hz plus 10 log₁₀B, the noise figure and the required SNR, so 1 dB of noise figure translates directly into 1 dB of sensitivity.

Noise figure is typically measured by the Y-factor method with a noise source. From the ratio Y of the output noise powers with the noise source on (hot) and off (ambient), and the noise source's excess noise ratio (ENR), the noise factor of the device under test is found. This is often built in as a function of noise figure analyzers and spectrum analyzers, and the correction for the instrument's own noise (second-stage correction) is also done with the Friis formula. Mismatch at each frequency and differences in noise source temperature are sources of error.

faq.q: What does a noise figure of 3 dB mean?
faq.a: It means that when the input noise is thermal noise at 290 K, passing through the circuit worsens the SNR by 3 dB (by half). The noise added by the circuit is as large as the input thermal noise.

faq.q: How do I convert between noise figure and noise temperature?
faq.a: Te = (10^(NF/10) − 1) × 290 K. An NF of 0.5 dB is about 35 K, 1 dB about 75 K, and 3 dB about 290 K.

faq.q: Does an amplifier with high gain also have a low noise figure?
faq.a: Not necessarily. Gain and noise figure are separate properties. A high first-stage gain does, however, reduce the effect that later-stage noise has on the total.

フリスの公式.desc: The formula F = F1 + (F2 − 1)/G1 + … that gives the overall noise factor of a multistage circuit. The noise and gain of the first stage largely set the total.

P1dB.desc: The 1 dB gain compression point: the power at which, as the input is raised, the gain has fallen 1 dB below its small-signal value. It marks the upper limit of linear operation.

IP3.desc: The third-order intercept point: the hypothetical power at which the extrapolated lines of the fundamental and IM3 cross. The higher it is, the more resistant the circuit is to intermodulation distortion.

about.p: When two signals at frequencies f1 and f2 enter an amplifier or mixer, third-order nonlinearity produces components at 2f1 − f2 and 2f2 − f1 (IM3). These appear right next to the original signals, so they cannot be removed by filtering. Raising the input by 1 dB increases the fundamental by 1 dB and IM3 by 3 dB, so the two straight lines on a dB plot, when extended, cross at some power. This is the third-order intercept point (IP3); the input-referred value is called IIP3 and the output-referred value OIP3, related by OIP3 = IIP3 + gain.

IP3 is a hypothetical point — the input cannot actually be driven that high — but it is convenient for estimating distortion. When each tone's output is Pout, the IM3 output is P_IM3 = 3·Pout − 2·OIP3, and its difference from the fundamental is 2(OIP3 − Pout) dB. For example, with an OIP3 of +30 dBm and an output of 0 dBm, IM3 is −60 dBm, and each 1 dB reduction in output widens the difference by 2 dB. In measurement, a two-tone test is done at inputs well below P1dB, and the calculation is made after confirming that the IM3 slope is 3.

In a receiver, IIP3 sets the tolerance to strong interferers and the noise floor sets the limit for weak signals. The spurious-free dynamic range set by third-order distortion is SFDR = (2/3)(IIP3 − noise floor); with an IIP3 of 0 dBm and a noise floor of −120 dBm it is 80 dB. For the overall IIP3 of a multistage circuit, later stages receive larger signals because of the gain before them, so, opposite to noise figure, the linearity of later stages matters. Raising the first-stage gain too much therefore improves noise figure but worsens IIP3, and the level plan is set as a compromise between the two.

faq.q: What is the difference between IP3 and P1dB?
faq.a: P1dB is the actual power at which the gain drops by 1 dB, while IP3 is the hypothetical power where the extrapolated lines of the fundamental and IM3 cross. Higher values of both indicate better linearity, but IP3 is used to estimate small-signal distortion and P1dB as a guide to the output limit.

faq.q: How many dB does IM3 increase for each dB of input?
faq.a: It increases by 3 dB per 1 dB of input. The fundamental increases by 1 dB, so the difference between the fundamental and IM3 shrinks by 2 dB per 1 dB of input.

faq.q: How do I convert between IIP3 and OIP3?
faq.a: OIP3 = IIP3 + gain (dB). With 15 dB of gain and an IIP3 of −5 dBm, the OIP3 is +10 dBm.

イメージ周波数.desc: The frequency on the opposite side of the local oscillator from the received frequency, which is converted to the same intermediate frequency. It lies 2×IF away from the received frequency.

位相雑音.desc: Noise spreading on both sides of a carrier because of fluctuations in an oscillator's phase. It is expressed as the power per hertz at each offset from the carrier, in dBc/Hz.

dBm.desc: Power expressed in dB relative to 1 mW. 0 dBm is 1 mW, +30 dBm is 1 W and −30 dBm is 1 µW; it is widely used to express RF power.

about.p: dBm is power expressed in dB relative to 1 mW: P [dBm] = 10 log₁₀(P/1 mW). 0 dBm is 1 mW, +10 dBm is 10 mW, +30 dBm is 1 W and −30 dBm is 1 µW; every 10 dB is a factor of 10 and every 3 dB roughly a factor of 2. In RF work, powers span an enormous range, from tens of watts at a transmitter to −100 dBm (0.1 pW) or less at a receiver input, so a logarithmic scale is convenient. There is also dBW, referenced to 1 W, with dBW = dBm − 30.

about.h: Rules for calculating with dB and dBm
about.p: dBm expresses an absolute power, while dB expresses a ratio. Gains and losses in dB can be added to or subtracted from dBm: a +10 dBm signal through an amplifier with 20 dB of gain becomes +30 dBm, and through a cable with 3 dB of loss becomes +7 dBm. dBm values, however, cannot be added to each other; two uncorrelated +10 dBm signals combine to 20 mW, about +13 dBm. The difference between two dBm values is in dB (a ratio); for example, the 10 dB difference between a received power of −80 dBm and a sensitivity of −90 dBm is the link margin.

dBm is a unit of power, so converting it to voltage requires the load impedance. Into 50 Ω, 0 dBm is about 0.224 V RMS and +10 dBm about 0.707 V. The conversion differs for 75 Ω or high-impedance systems, so be careful. dBc, the ratio to a reference signal such as the carrier, is also widely used; spurs at −60 dBc are 60 dB below the carrier. Noise per unit bandwidth is expressed in dBm/Hz, and phase noise in dBc/Hz.

faq.q: How many watts is 0 dBm?
faq.a: 1 mW (0.001 W). +30 dBm is 1 W, +40 dBm is 10 W, and −30 dBm is 1 µW.

faq.q: When is it OK to add dBm values?
faq.a: Adding or subtracting dB (gain or loss) to or from dBm is a correct calculation. Adding dBm values to each other means multiplying powers, so when combining two signals, convert them to mW first and add.

faq.q: How many volts is 0 dBm in 50 Ω?
faq.a: About 0.224 V RMS, or about 0.316 V peak. From P = V²/R, V = √(0.001 × 50).

ミキサ.desc: A circuit that multiplies two signals to produce their sum and difference frequencies. In a receiver, it produces the intermediate frequency from the received signal and the local oscillator.

Q値.desc: A value expressing the sharpness of a resonance. It is proportional to the ratio of energy stored to energy lost, and for a resonant circuit it is the center frequency divided by the 3 dB bandwidth.

共振周波数.desc: The frequency at which the reactances of L and C cancel, f = 1/(2π√LC). At series resonance the impedance is minimum, and at parallel resonance it is maximum.

バターワース特性.desc: A filter response with the flattest possible passband amplitude. It has no ripple, and above the cutoff frequency an nth-order filter attenuates by about 6n dB per octave.

水晶振動子.desc: A component that uses the mechanical resonance of quartz through the piezoelectric effect. Its Q is very high and its frequency varies little with temperature, so it serves as the reference for stable oscillators.

PLL.desc: Phase-locked loop: a circuit that divides the VCO output, compares its phase with a reference signal, and produces a stable frequency such as N times the reference.

VCO.desc: Voltage-controlled oscillator: an oscillator whose frequency can be changed by a tuning voltage, most often by varying the capacitance of a varactor diode with voltage.

ダイポールアンテナ.desc: An antenna made of two conductors fed at the center. The half-wave dipole has a radiation resistance of about 73 Ω and a gain of 2.15 dBi, and is used as a reference.

about.p: A dipole antenna is the most basic antenna, made of two conductors in a straight line fed at the center. One whose total length is a half wavelength is called a half-wave dipole; the current along the conductors is maximum at the center and zero at the ends. It radiates most strongly at right angles to the conductors and not at all along them, giving a figure-eight pattern. A thin half-wave dipole has a radiation resistance of about 73 Ω and a slightly inductive reactance, so in practice the total length is cut a few percent shorter than a half wavelength to make it resonate.

about.h: The dipole as a gain reference
about.p: The gain of a half-wave dipole is 2.15 dB greater than that of an isotropic antenna, 2.15 dBi. Because it is a convenient reference among real antennas, gain referenced to the dipole, dBd, is also used, with dBi = dBd + 2.15. A Yagi–Uda antenna places directors and a reflector in front of and behind a dipole driven element to concentrate the radiation in one direction. Gain is quoted against either reference, so when comparing datasheet values you need to check whether it is dBi or dBd.

Replacing one half of a dipole with a large conducting plane (the ground or a car roof) gives a λ/4 monopole, with the image in the plane doing the work of the missing half. Its radiation resistance is about 36.5 Ω, half that of the dipole, and it is used for whip antennas on portable devices and similar. A folded dipole, made by folding a half-wave conductor back into two parallel wires, has a radiation resistance about four times larger, about 292 Ω, and a somewhat wider bandwidth. A dipole is a balanced antenna, so when it is fed with unbalanced coaxial cable a balun is inserted to keep current from flowing on the outside of the cable.

faq.q: How is the length of a half-wave dipole determined?
faq.a: Find the wavelength from λ = c/f and take half of it. At 150 MHz that is 1 m, but in practice it is cut a few percent shorter, depending on the conductor thickness, to make it resonate.

faq.q: What is the impedance of a half-wave dipole?
faq.a: About 73 Ω for a half-wave dipole of thin wire. A λ/4 monopole has half that, about 36.5 Ω, and a folded dipole about 292 Ω.

faq.q: How do I convert between dBi and dBd?
faq.a: dBi = dBd + 2.15. An antenna of 10 dBd is 12.15 dBi.

dBi.desc: Antenna gain in dB relative to an isotropic antenna. It is related to dBd, referenced to a half-wave dipole, by dBi = dBd + 2.15.

実効開口面積.desc: The effective area over which an antenna extracts power from an incoming wave. It is related to gain by Ae = Gλ²/4π.

自由空間伝搬損失.desc: The loss between isotropic antennas caused by radio waves spreading out spherically. L = 20 log₁₀(4πd/λ); it is proportional to the square of distance and of frequency.

偏波.desc: The direction of a radio wave's electric field and how it changes. There are linear and circular polarizations, and a polarization mismatch between transmitter and receiver lowers the received power.

フレネルゾーン.desc: A region shaped like an ellipsoid of revolution with the transmitter and receiver at its foci; the region where the path difference is within half a wavelength is the first Fresnel zone. Obstacles inside it increase loss.

レーダー方程式.desc: The equation expressing a radar's received power in terms of transmit power, antenna gain, wavelength, target cross section and range. The received power is inversely proportional to the fourth power of the range.

QAM.desc: Quadrature amplitude modulation: digital modulation that amplitude-modulates two orthogonal carriers and combines them, carrying information in both amplitude and phase.

シンボルレート.desc: The number of symbols (units of modulation) sent per second, in baud. With M-ary modulation, the bit rate is log₂M times the symbol rate.

ロールオフ率.desc: The value α expressing how far a band-limiting filter extends beyond the Nyquist minimum bandwidth. When transmitted on a carrier, the bandwidth is Rs(1 + α).

Eb/N0.desc: The ratio of signal energy per bit to the noise power spectral density. It is used to compare the error rates of schemes with different bit rates fairly.

EVM.desc: Error vector magnitude: a measure of modulation accuracy that expresses the deviation of received or transmitted constellation points from their ideal positions as an RMS ratio.

OFDM.desc: Orthogonal frequency-division multiplexing: a scheme that divides data among many mutually orthogonal subcarriers. It is robust against multipath.

表皮効果.desc: The phenomenon in which, the higher the frequency, the more AC current concentrates near the surface of a conductor. The thickness carrying the current is the skin depth, inversely proportional to √f.

about.h: Why current gathers at the surface
about.p: When AC current flows in a conductor, the changing magnetic field around the current induces an EMF inside the conductor that acts to cancel the current in the center. The higher the frequency, the stronger this effect, and the current concentrates near the surface of the conductor. This is the skin effect, and the depth at which the current density falls to 1/e (about 37%) of its surface value is called the skin depth, δ = √(ρ/(πfμ)). For copper it is about 9 mm at 50 Hz, about 66 µm at 1 MHz, about 6.6 µm at 100 MHz and about 0.66 µm at 10 GHz, thinning in inverse proportion to the square root of frequency.

Because current flows only within roughly one skin depth, the RF resistance of a conductor is much larger than its DC resistance and increases in proportion to the square root of frequency. For the same reason, the conductor loss of a transmission line rises as √f, and together with dielectric loss, which rises in proportion to frequency, trace loss grows at higher frequencies. Making the conductor thicker helps only a little, since the center carries almost no current. That is why RF coils use Litz wire, made of many fine strands twisted together, and high-power conductors are sometimes hollow tubes.

When the skin depth falls to a few µm or less, the condition of the conductor surface has a large effect on loss. Copper foil on printed circuit boards is roughened to improve adhesion to the dielectric, but when the roughness is comparable to the skin depth, the current path gets longer and loss increases. High-speed and RF boards therefore use low-profile copper foil with little roughness. Also, if the surface is plated with a metal of high resistivity that is also magnetic, such as nickel, the current flows in that layer and loss increases. The effectiveness of a shield is likewise set by the plate thickness relative to the skin depth.

faq.q: How is the skin depth calculated?
faq.a: δ = √(ρ/(πfμ)). For copper (ρ = 1.7×10⁻⁸ Ω·m, μ = 4π×10⁻⁷ H/m), it is about 6.6 µm at 100 MHz.

faq.q: What happens to the skin depth when the frequency quadruples?
faq.a: It halves, since √4 = 2. The current-carrying thickness is halved, so the RF resistance roughly doubles.

faq.q: Does the skin effect occur at DC?
faq.a: No. At DC the magnetic field does not change, so no EMF is induced, and the current flows uniformly over the whole cross section.

マイクロストリップ線路.desc: A transmission line formed by a signal trace on the surface of a substrate and a ground plane on the back. Part of the electric field passes through the air, so the effective relative permittivity is lower than the substrate's.

差動伝送.desc: A method of sending information as the difference between opposite-phase signals on two lines. It is robust against common-mode noise and radiates little.

コモンモード.desc: The component flowing in the same direction and phase on two or more lines. Because the currents do not cancel, it is a main cause of unwanted radiation from cables.

TDR.desc: Time-domain reflectometry: launching a step into a line and observing the timing and size of the reflections to find the location and size of impedance discontinuities.

アイパターン.desc: A plot of a digital waveform overlaid one bit period at a time (also called an eye pattern). The height and width of the eye-shaped opening are used to evaluate the margin against noise and jitter.

EIRP.desc: Equivalent isotropically radiated power: the transmitter output minus feed line loss plus antenna gain. It expresses the effective transmit strength in the direction of maximum radiation.

リンクマージン.desc: The difference between the received power found in a link budget and the receiver sensitivity. It represents the allowance for drops in received power from fading, rain and other causes.

ミリ波.desc: Radio waves with frequencies of 30–300 GHz and wavelengths of 1–10 mm. Wide bandwidths and small antennas are available, but propagation loss and attenuation by the atmosphere and rain are large.

降雨減衰.desc: The weakening of radio waves by absorption and scattering in raindrops. It starts to become noticeable above roughly 10 GHz and grows with frequency and rain intensity.

静止軌道.desc: An orbit about 36,000 km above the equator with the same period as the earth's rotation. From the ground the satellite appears stationary, and it is used for communications and broadcasting.

G/T.desc: The ratio of receive antenna gain to system noise temperature, expressed in dB/K. It is the figure of merit of a receiving station; the larger it is, the weaker the signals it can receive.

方形導波管.desc: A hollow metal pipe with a rectangular cross section that carries microwaves with low loss. Its fundamental mode is TE10, and frequencies below fc = c/(2a), set by the broad dimension a, do not propagate.

about.h: How waves travel in a waveguide
about.p: A rectangular waveguide is a hollow metal pipe with a rectangular cross section. The electromagnetic wave traveling inside can be thought of as advancing along the axis while bouncing obliquely off the walls. With no second conductor, as a coaxial line has, the TEM mode — with both electric and magnetic fields perpendicular to the direction of travel — cannot exist, and only TE and TM modes propagate. Every mode has a cutoff frequency below which it does not propagate; below cutoff, the fields simply decay exponentially from the entrance.

about.h: The TE10 mode and the usable frequency range
about.p: The fundamental mode, with the lowest cutoff frequency, is TE10; its cutoff is fc = c/(2a), where the broad dimension a is exactly half a wavelength. The next lowest modes are TE20 and TE01, and with the standard proportions a = 2b both are at 2fc. The single-mode range where only TE10 propagates is therefore fc to 2fc, and in practice waveguides are used from about 1.25fc to 1.9fc to avoid the large loss and dispersion near cutoff. Standard dimensions are defined for each frequency band; for example, X-band waveguide has a broad dimension of about 23 mm.

about.h: Guide wavelength and advantages over coaxial line
about.p: The wavelength inside a waveguide (the guide wavelength) is λg = λ0/√(1 − (fc/f)²), longer than the free-space wavelength. The phase velocity is faster than light and the group velocity, at which energy travels, is slower than light; both change with frequency, so a waveguide is a dispersive line. With no center conductor, conductor loss is low, and with no insulator needed it can handle high power, so waveguides are used in radar transmitters, satellite earth stations, particle accelerators and similar. On the other hand, the usable band is less than an octave, and waveguides are bulky and hard to bend.

faq.q: Can DC or low frequencies pass through a waveguide?
faq.a: No. A waveguide has a high-pass character that does not carry frequencies below cutoff, so not only DC but any signal below the TE10 cutoff is attenuated near the entrance.

faq.q: Why are waveguides used in the TE10 mode?
faq.a: Because its cutoff frequency is the lowest, allowing a frequency range in which it alone propagates. If several modes propagate at once, mode conversion at discontinuities disturbs the response. Its electric field also points in a single direction, which makes polarization easy to handle.

faq.q: What happens if a waveguide is filled with a dielectric?
faq.a: For the same dimensions, the cutoff frequency drops by a factor of 1/√εr, and the guide wavelength also gets shorter. This allows a smaller waveguide, but dielectric loss is added.

カットオフ周波数.desc: The lowest frequency at which a given mode begins to propagate in a waveguide or similar structure. Below it the wave does not propagate and decays exponentially. For the TE10 mode of a rectangular waveguide, fc = c/(2a).

TE10モード.desc: The fundamental mode of a rectangular waveguide. Its electric field points only perpendicular to the broad walls and forms a single half-wavelength peak across the broad dimension. It has the lowest cutoff frequency.

管内波長.desc: The wavelength along the axis of a wave traveling in a waveguide. λg = λ0/√(1 − (fc/f)²); it is longer than the free-space wavelength and grows longer as cutoff is approached.

空洞共振器.desc: A resonator in which a standing electromagnetic wave is set up inside a cavity enclosed by metal walls. When air-filled, its loss comes almost entirely from skin currents in the walls, giving high Qs of several thousand to tens of thousands.

アイソレータ.desc: A nonreciprocal device that passes signals in the forward direction with little loss and strongly attenuates them in the reverse direction. It uses ferrite and protects oscillators and amplifiers from waves reflected by the load.

about.h: A device that passes signals one way only
about.p: An isolator is a two-port device that passes signals from port 1 to port 2 with a small insertion loss (usually 1 dB or less) and gives a large attenuation (isolation) of about 20 dB or more from port 2 to port 1. Circuits made only of resistors and capacitors have S21 = S12 by the reciprocity theorem, so they cannot produce this nonreciprocal behavior. The isolator achieves it using the property that, in a ferrite under a DC magnetic field, electromagnetic waves propagate differently depending on their direction.

about.h: Relation to the circulator, and types
about.p: A common form is a three-port circulator with a matched termination on one port. Forward signals pass straight through, while reflected waves coming back are routed by the circulator into the termination and absorbed as heat. In waveguide there are also field-displacement types, which use the way the field distribution in the ferrite shifts depending on the direction of travel, and types that use rotation of the plane of polarization (Faraday rotation). For any type, choose with attention to the usable frequency band and how much reflected power the termination can handle.

A typical use is between the output of an oscillator or power amplifier and a load such as an antenna. It absorbs waves reflected by load mismatch, preventing the oscillator frequency from being dragged by the load (frequency pulling) and protecting the amplifier's output devices from damage by reflections. In measurement too, inserting one between the source and the device under test improves the match seen by the source and reduces measurement error. The effective return loss seen by the oscillator can be thought of as the load's return loss plus the isolation.

faq.q: What is the difference between an isolator and a circulator?
faq.a: A circulator has three ports and passes signals in turn in the direction 1 → 2 → 3 → 1. An isolator has two ports and simply passes signals in one direction. Terminating one port of a circulator turns it into an isolator.

faq.q: Is it OK to place an isolator near a magnet?
faq.a: Care is needed. Its characteristics are set by the DC magnetic field applied to the ferrite, so strong external magnetic fields or nearby magnetic materials can change them.

faq.q: Does an isolator eliminate the reflection itself?
faq.a: No. The load keeps reflecting; the isolator just absorbs the reflected wave so it does not return to the source. The power reaching the load is still reduced by the amount reflected.

PINダイオード.desc: A diode with a high-resistivity intrinsic (i) layer between its p and n layers. At RF it acts as a small resistance set by the current under forward bias and a small capacitance under reverse bias, and is used in switches and attenuators.

パワーセンサ.desc: A sensor for measuring RF power. Thermal types such as thermocouple sensors indicate average power regardless of waveform, while diode-detector types are highly sensitive but used within their square-law range.

距離分解能.desc: The smallest range difference at which two targets in the same direction can be distinguished. For a simple pulse it is cτ/2; with pulse compression or FMCW it is c/(2B), set by the bandwidth B.

パルス繰り返し周波数.desc: The number of pulses a pulsed radar transmits per second (PRF). The unambiguous range is c/(2·PRF); raising the PRF shortens that range and widens the range of measurable velocities.

パルス圧縮.desc: A technique that transmits a long pulse with modulation such as a chirp and compresses it into a short pulse with a matched filter at the receiver. It maintains detection range while achieving a range resolution of c/(2B).

ドップラー周波数.desc: The frequency shift in the echo from a moving target. In radar it acts on the round trip, so fd = 2v/λ, proportional only to the radial velocity component.

FMCWレーダー.desc: A radar that transmits a continuous wave whose frequency changes linearly and finds range from the frequency difference with the echo (the beat frequency). It is the dominant approach for automotive millimeter-wave radar.

about.h: Using the frequency change as a clock
about.p: An FMCW radar transmits a continuous wave whose frequency changes linearly with time (a chirp). The echo from a target returns after the round-trip time τ = 2R/c, so by the time it is received the transmit frequency has already moved on. Multiplying the transmitted wave and the echo in a mixer gives their difference frequency, the beat frequency fb = S·τ, where S is the slope of the frequency change. The beat frequency is proportional to range, so when the beat signal is analyzed with an FFT, the frequency axis directly becomes the range axis.

about.h: What sets resolution and maximum range
about.p: Range resolution is set by the sweep bandwidth B: ΔR = c/(2B). A 1 GHz bandwidth gives 15 cm, and 4 GHz about 3.75 cm. The maximum measurable range, on the other hand, is set by the sampling rate of the ADC that captures the beat signal and by the chirp slope. Unlike pulsed radar, transmitting and receiving happen at the same time, so only a low peak power is needed, and the beat signal is at a low frequency of a few MHz, so it can be processed with inexpensive ADCs. This makes FMCW well suited to small, low-power radars.

Automotive radars transmit many short chirps at regular intervals. When a target moves, the phase of the signal in the same range bin rotates slightly from chirp to chirp, so a second FFT across the sequence of chirps gives the Doppler frequency and hence the velocity. The target's azimuth is then found from the phase differences between multiple receive antennas. In MIMO configurations that also use multiple transmit antennas, the transmit-receive combinations act like a virtual array of many antennas, raising angular resolution on a small circuit board.

faq.q: Can an FMCW radar see stationary objects?
faq.a: Yes. The beat frequency is set by range, so stationary objects with zero Doppler frequency are also detected by their range. A Doppler radar transmitting a constant-frequency continuous wave cannot measure the range of stationary objects.

faq.q: What changes if the chirp slope is made steeper?
faq.a: The beat frequency is higher for the same range. Shortening the sweep time without changing the bandwidth shortens the interval between velocity measurements, but faster ADCs are needed to capture the beat signal.

faq.q: Are strong nearby reflections a problem?
faq.a: Yes. Strong reflections from the bumper and similar, or transmit leakage, can saturate the receiver, and phase noise can bury weak distant targets. That is why isolation between transmit and receive antennas and low-phase-noise oscillators are important.

ビート周波数.desc: The difference frequency that appears when signals at two frequencies are mixed. In FMCW radar it is the frequency difference between the transmitted wave and the echo, and it is proportional to the range to the target.

レーダー断面積.desc: A quantity (RCS, symbol σ) that expresses how strongly a target reflects toward the radar as the area of an equivalent target scattering isotropically. It varies greatly with shape, orientation and frequency.

about.p: The radar cross section (RCS) σ expresses how strongly the radio waves hitting a target come back toward the radar. It is defined as the area such that, if the target intercepted power over σ and scattered it equally in all directions, an echo as strong as the real one would return to the radar. Its unit is m², often expressed in dBsm, relative to 1 m²; 10 dBsm is 10 m². σ is not the physical size itself but a measure of how the target reflects, so targets of the same size can have very different values.

about.h: Dependence on shape, orientation and frequency
about.p: A flat metal plate seen head-on has an enormous σ = 4πA²/λ², but tilting it only slightly lowers it dramatically. A corner reflector, made of three plates joined at right angles, returns waves arriving over a wide range of angles back in their original direction, so it has a large σ despite being small and is used on boats and as a calibration target. A metal sphere much larger than the wavelength has σ = πa² and serves as an orientation-independent reference target. For complex targets such as aircraft, σ can change by tens of times with a small change in viewing angle, which causes the echo to fluctuate.

In the radar equation the received power is proportional to σ/R⁴, so the maximum detection range is proportional to the fourth root of σ. Cutting σ to 1/100 (20 dB) reduces the detection range only to about 0.32 times, and conversely, doubling the detection range for the same σ requires a 16-fold (12 dB) improvement in transmit power or sensitivity. Stealth technology reduces σ by shaping to deflect reflections away from the radar and by using radar-absorbing materials to reduce the reflection itself. In automotive radar, pedestrians have a much smaller σ than cars, which makes them harder to detect.

faq.q: Does a larger radar cross section mean a larger target?
faq.a: Not necessarily. σ is set by the direction and strength of the reflection, so a small corner reflector can have a larger σ than a large aircraft.

faq.q: Does radar cross section change with frequency?
faq.a: In many cases, yes. For a flat plate it is inversely proportional to λ², and for objects about the size of the wavelength it rises and falls greatly because of resonance. Frequency-independent examples, such as a sufficiently large metal sphere, are limited.

faq.q: What is dBsm?
faq.a: Radar cross section expressed in dB relative to 1 m². 0 dBsm is 1 m², 20 dBsm is 100 m², and −10 dBsm is 0.1 m².

MIMOレーダー.desc: A radar that uses multiple transmit and receive antennas and forms a virtual array from the transmit-receive combinations. With three transmit and four receive antennas, an aperture equivalent to 12 elements can be obtained, depending on the layout.

スペクトラムアナライザ.desc: An instrument that displays an input signal as power versus frequency. The basic approach sweeps a local oscillator and measures through an RBW filter at the IF; it is used to measure spurs and noise.

about.h: How a swept spectrum analyzer works
about.p: A typical spectrum analyzer is a superheterodyne receiver whose local oscillator frequency is swept. The input signal is converted to an IF by a mixer, passed through the resolution bandwidth (RBW) filter, detected, and displayed on the vertical axis. As the local oscillator frequency changes, so does the input frequency that passes the filter, drawing a spectrum with frequency on the horizontal axis and power on the vertical. Most current models handle everything from the IF onward with digital signal processing, and also use FFT methods to analyze a wide band at once.

The noise power displayed on screen is set by thermal noise of −174 dBm/Hz plus the instrument's noise figure and the RBW bandwidth. Cutting the RBW to 1/10 lowers the noise by 10 dB while leaving the display of a sine-wave signal unchanged, so weak signals emerge from the noise. However, the sweep time increases in inverse proportion to the square of the RBW. The noise displayed with the input terminated is called the displayed average noise level (DANL), and it is a guide to the smallest measurable signal. Adding a preamplifier lowers the noise figure and with it the DANL.

When large signals enter the first mixer, it generates harmonics and intermodulation distortion of its own and displays signals that are not actually present at the input. Increasing the input attenuator reduces the signal reaching the mixer and lowers this distortion, but raises the displayed noise level correspondingly. When measuring weak distortion near a strong signal, the basic practice is to choose the attenuation where noise and distortion balance. Whether displayed distortion comes from the instrument can be checked by changing the attenuation and seeing whether the displayed level changes.

faq.q: How does a spectrum analyzer differ from an oscilloscope?
faq.a: An oscilloscope has time on the horizontal axis and shows voltage waveforms. A spectrum analyzer has frequency on the horizontal axis and shows how much power is at each frequency. Because it can measure with a narrow RBW, it can see far smaller signals and spurs than an oscilloscope.

faq.q: Is the displayed value the true power of the signal?
faq.a: For a sine wave well above the noise and within the RBW, it is nearly the true power. Signals close to the noise level are displayed larger because the noise adds to them, and the display of noise itself changes with the detection method (log average or RMS average). Losses in cables and attenuators also need to be corrected.

faq.q: Is there a limit on the power that can be applied to the input?
faq.a: Yes. A maximum input power that will not damage the input attenuator or mixer is specified, and there is also a limit on DC voltage. When measuring a transmitter's output, reduce it sufficiently with an attenuator or directional coupler before applying it.

分解能帯域幅.desc: The bandwidth of a spectrum analyzer's IF filter (RBW). The narrower it is, the better closely spaced signals are separated and the lower the displayed noise, but the sweep time gets longer.

表示平均雑音レベル.desc: The noise level displayed on a spectrum analyzer when its input is terminated (DANL). It is set by the instrument's noise figure and the RBW, and is a guide to the smallest measurable signal.

ベクトルネットワークアナライザ.desc: An instrument (VNA) that measures the S-parameters of a network in both magnitude and phase. It measures the incident, reflected and transmitted waves separately and removes systematic errors such as directivity by calibration.

about.p: A vector network analyzer (VNA) sends a signal into the device under test and measures the waves reflected back and transmitted through, comparing them with the incident wave. Because it measures phase as well as magnitude, it obtains S11 and S21 as complex numbers, from which impedance, group delay and traces on the Smith chart can be derived. Inside are a signal source, directional couplers (bridges) that separate the incident and reflected waves, and receivers that measure each wave; it sweeps the frequency and calculates the ratios at each point. It is called "vector" to distinguish it from scalar network analyzers, which measure magnitude only.

Raw measurements contain systematic errors because the internal couplers have finite directivity, the test ports are not perfectly matched, and the cables and receivers have frequency responses. The VNA treats these as coefficients of an error model, determines the coefficients by measuring calibration standards of known characteristics, and removes them by calculation. A one-port reflection uses a three-term error model — directivity, source match and reflection tracking — and two-port SOLT calibration uses a 12-term model. The calibrated plane (the reference plane) becomes the reference for the measured values.

Receiver noise, the repeatability of each connector reconnection, and drift from temperature changes after calibration cannot be removed by calibration. Noise is reduced by narrowing the IF bandwidth or averaging, connectors are tightened to a set torque with a torque wrench, and calibration and measurement are done with a stable temperature. Also, the correctness of a calibration depends on the definitions of the calibration standards, so the type of standards must match the calibration kit settings. When measuring on a board inside a fixture, the fixture's contribution is subtracted by de-embedding.

faq.q: How often is calibration needed?
faq.a: Recalibrate whenever the measurement conditions change, such as frequency range, number of points, IF bandwidth or cables. Even with the same conditions, temperature changes and the passage of time cause drift, so before measurements that need accuracy, recalibrate or check with a verification standard.

faq.q: Can't a spectrum analyzer measure this instead?
faq.a: A spectrum analyzer with a tracking generator can measure the magnitude of transmission, but it cannot measure phase and its error correction is limited. Accurate measurement of impedance, group delay or high isolation requires a VNA.

faq.q: What does the IF bandwidth affect?
faq.a: The size of the receiver noise and the sweep speed. Narrowing it reduces trace scatter and allows smaller transmission to be measured, but the sweep takes longer.

SOLT校正.desc: A calibration method that measures short, open, load and thru standards to determine and remove a VNA's systematic errors (12 terms for two ports).

Yファクタ法.desc: A method of finding noise figure as F = ENR/(Y − 1) from the ratio Y of the output noise powers with a noise source on and off. The noise figure is found without knowing the gain of the device under test.

ENR.desc: The excess noise ratio of a noise source, ENR = (Th − 290)/290, from its noise temperature Th when on and the reference temperature of 290 K, usually given in dB. It is used in the Y-factor method.

ミスマッチ不確かさ.desc: The uncertainty in a power measurement caused by multiple reflections from the mismatch between a source and a power sensor. The phases are unknown, so it is estimated as a range of 20 log₁₀(1 ± |Γs||ΓL|) dB.

導通角.desc: The portion of one cycle of a sinusoidal input during which current flows in the transistor. Class A is 360°, Class B 180°, Class AB in between, and Class C less than 180°; the narrower it is, the higher the efficiency.

電力付加効率.desc: The ratio of the power an amplifier adds to its input to the DC power (PAE). PAE = (Pout − Pin)/PDC; the lower the gain, the further it falls below the drain efficiency.

PAPR.desc: The ratio of a signal's instantaneous peak power to its average power. It is large for OFDM, and amplifiers are run with the average output lowered according to the PAPR to avoid saturation.

AM-PM変換.desc: Amplifier nonlinearity in which the output phase changes with input amplitude. It rotates the high-amplitude points of QAM signals and degrades EVM. It is treated together with AM-AM, which describes gain compression.

DPD.desc: Digital predistortion: a linearization method that applies the inverse of a power amplifier's characteristics to the digital signal to be transmitted, so that the response after the amplifier is linear.

about.p: OFDM and high-order QAM signals vary greatly in amplitude, so the AM-AM (gain compression) and AM-PM (phase shift) nonlinearities of a power amplifier turn directly into distortion. The distortion degrades EVM as displaced constellation points and spreads the spectrum into adjacent channels through intermodulation. Backing the amplifier off heavily and using only its linear range reduces distortion, but efficiency drops sharply and heat and power consumption rise. Linearization techniques are used to meet distortion specifications while operating at an efficient operating point.

DPD adds distortion opposite to the amplifier's characteristics at the baseband digital stage. If the amplifier's gain drops at large amplitudes, the signal is made larger beforehand at those amplitudes, and if the phase shifts, it is rotated back by that amount. Part of the amplifier output is converted back to a digital signal by an observation receiver, compared with the intended signal, and the coefficients of the inverse model are updated adaptively. Because it is done in digital processing, it can track changes in characteristics with temperature and aging, which is an advantage.

DPD corrects the response within the range the amplifier can deliver, so it cannot produce peaks beyond saturated output, and it is combined with backoff matched to the signal's PAPR and with clipping that trims the peaks. With wideband signals, thermal effects and the time constants of bias circuits produce memory effects, in which the output depends on slightly earlier inputs as well. In that case a model that also uses past inputs, such as a memory polynomial, is needed instead of an inverse characteristic set only by amplitude. The output must be observed over a bandwidth several times the band to be corrected, so the performance of the observation path also affects the result.

faq.q: How does DPD differ from analog linearization?
faq.a: Feedforward is an analog method that extracts the amplifier's distortion and cancels it in antiphase; it is accurate but needs an auxiliary amplifier, which lowers efficiency. DPD can correct with digital processing alone and preserves efficiency more easily, so it is widely used in base station transmitters.

faq.q: Does DPD eliminate the need for backoff?
faq.a: No. Peaks beyond saturated output cannot be corrected, so backoff matched to the PAPR remains. What DPD does is allow linear use up to close to saturation, reducing the backoff required.

faq.q: Are Doherty amplifiers and DPD used together?
faq.a: Often. A Doherty amplifier has high efficiency at backoff, but load modulation tends to make its characteristics nonlinear, so it is used with DPD correcting that nonlinearity.

ロードプル.desc: A method of measuring output power and efficiency under large-signal conditions while varying the load impedance at the transistor's output. The results are drawn as contours on a Smith chart to find the optimum load for a power amplifier.

ドハティ増幅器.desc: A power amplifier that combines a Class AB main amplifier and a Class C peaking amplifier through a λ/4 line, using the peaking amplifier's current to change the main amplifier's load (load modulation). It stays efficient even when the output is reduced.

about.p: A Doherty amplifier places a main amplifier biased in Class AB and a peaking amplifier biased in Class C side by side, combining the main amplifier's output through a λ/4 line at a common node. On the input side, a λ/4 phase delay is also inserted on the peaking amplifier's path so that the two outputs are in phase at the combining node. At low output the peaking amplifier is off and only the main amplifier operates. As the output grows and the peaking amplifier turns on, both amplifiers inject current into the combining node, and at maximum output both operate into their optimum loads.

A λ/4 line transforms an impedance ZL at its far end into Z0²/ZL. In the symmetrical design, the load at the combining node is half the optimum load, and the characteristic impedance of the λ/4 line equals the optimum load. With the peaking amplifier off, the main amplifier sees twice its optimum load, so its voltage saturates at half the current, and efficiency is at its maximum. When the peaking amplifier injects current, the apparent impedance at the combining node rises, and the main amplifier's load seen through the λ/4 line falls. Through this load modulation, the main amplifier increases its output while its voltage remains saturated, maintaining high efficiency.

An ideal symmetrical Doherty amplifier reaches maximum efficiency at two points, at maximum output and 6 dB below maximum, and stays highly efficient in between. This property is very valuable in base stations, where signals with a PAPR of about 6–10 dB are used with the average output backed off. Asymmetrical designs with a larger peaking amplifier can place the efficiency peak at even deeper backoff. On the other hand, the λ/4 line tends to narrow the bandwidth, and the turn-on of the Class C peaking amplifier introduces nonlinearity, so it is generally used together with DPD.

faq.q: Why is it called "Doherty"?
faq.a: It is named after W. H. Doherty, who devised the scheme in 1936. It was originally conceived for vacuum-tube AM broadcast transmitters to keep efficiency high as the output varied.

faq.q: Is it used in mobile handsets too?
faq.a: Its main use is in base station transmitters. Handsets mostly use schemes that vary the supply voltage with the output level (APT, which follows the average output, and envelope tracking, which follows the signal envelope), though some do use Doherty amplifiers.

faq.q: Can a Doherty amplifier alone meet distortion specifications?
faq.a: In most cases, no. The turn-on of the peaking amplifier and load modulation tend to make its characteristics nonlinear, so it is linearized with DPD.

E級増幅器.desc: An amplifier that uses a single transistor as a switch, with a shunt capacitance and load network that bring the voltage to zero at the instant of turn-on (zero-voltage switching). Its theoretical efficiency is 100%.

アレーファクタ.desc: The factor in an array antenna's radiation pattern that is set only by the element positions and the amplitude and phase given to each element. The overall pattern is the product of the element pattern and the array factor.

フェーズドアレーアンテナ.desc: An array antenna that changes the direction of its beam without moving, by electronically changing the phases given to its many elements. It is used in radar and millimeter-wave communication.

グレーティングローブ.desc: A lobe as strong as the main beam that appears in another direction when the element spacing is too wide. Avoiding it up to a scan angle θ requires d < λ/(1 + |sinθ|).

about.p: The waves from equally spaced elements all line up and reinforce one another in any direction where the phase shift between neighbors (the sum of the feed phase difference and the path difference) is an integer multiple of 360°. The main beam is the direction where that shift is zero, but if the element spacing is wide, another direction where the shift is exactly ±360° comes into visible space (−90° to +90°). There the waves reinforce under exactly the same conditions as in the main beam, so a lobe as strong as the main beam appears. This is the grating lobe, the same mechanism by which a diffraction grating produces several orders of light. It can also be seen as aliasing caused by sampling space discretely with elements.

The directions of the grating lobes are given by sinθg = sinθ0 ± mλ/d (m = 1, 2, …). When the beam points to broadside (θ0 = 0), d < λ makes |sinθg| > 1, so there is no real direction and no grating lobe appears. Scanning the beam to θ0 brings the lobe on the opposite side toward visible space, so the condition tightens to d < λ/(1 + |sinθ0|). The spacing at which none appears even when scanning to ±90° is d ≤ λ/2, which is why many phased arrays use an element spacing of about half a wavelength. For example, scanning to ±60° at 10 GHz gives an upper limit of about 16 mm.

Wider element spacing lets the same aperture be built with fewer elements and phase shifters, which helps with cost. So in applications where the scan range is narrowly limited, the spacing is sometimes widened right up to the limit. In practice the main beam and grating lobes have width, so the spacing is chosen slightly narrower than the limit to keep the skirt of the lobe out of visible space. Other methods use the small element pattern at oblique angles to weaken grating lobes, or deliberately make the element positions irregular to spread a strong lobe into low sidelobes. For a wideband array, the condition is checked at the wavelength of the highest frequency.

faq.q: How do grating lobes differ from sidelobes?
faq.a: Sidelobes are weak lobes around the main beam; with uniform amplitude they are about 13 dB below the main beam. Grating lobes appear when the element spacing is too wide and are as strong as the main beam.

faq.q: Do grating lobes disappear if I add more elements?
faq.a: No. Adding elements only makes each lobe narrower; the direction and strength of the grating lobes are set by the element spacing and wavelength. To remove them, the element spacing must be narrowed.

faq.q: Is there any benefit to spacing elements closer than half a wavelength?
faq.a: There is no longer any concern about grating lobes, but more elements are needed for the same aperture and mutual coupling between elements becomes stronger. So the usual choice is the widest spacing that still meets the condition for the required scan range.

移相器.desc: A circuit that changes the phase of the signal passing through it. In a phased array it sets the phase of each element to scan the beam. The step of an n-bit digital phase shifter is 360°/2ⁿ.

ビームスクイント.desc: The change in beam direction of an array scanned with phase shifters when the frequency departs from the design value. The higher the frequency, the more the beam moves toward broadside.

真の時間遅延.desc: A scanning method that gives each element a time delay rather than a phase (TTD). The delay from the path difference, d sinθ/c, does not depend on frequency, so beam squint does not occur.

ビームフォーミング.desc: A technique that applies weights (amplitude and phase) to the signals of several elements and combines them so that radio waves reinforce in a particular direction. There are analog, digital and hybrid schemes.

about.p: Beamforming multiplies the signals of several antenna elements by complex weights (amplitude and phase) and adds them, reinforcing waves in the intended direction and weakening waves in other directions. On transmit, the weights are chosen so that the waves from the elements are in phase in the target direction; on receive, so that waves arriving from the target direction are in phase at the combining point. Changing only the phases changes the beam direction, and changing the amplitude distribution changes the sidelobe level and beamwidth. A zero of gain (a null) can also be pointed toward interference, and the technique is used widely in radar, mobile base stations, satellite terminals and more.

Analog beamforming applies the weights with RF phase shifters and variable attenuators before combining, so a single transceiver chain follows. Power consumption and parts are kept low, but only one beam can be formed at a time. Digital beamforming has a transceiver chain with an ADC and DAC for each element and applies the weights in signal processing. Several beams can be formed at once from the same data, and time delays can be applied freely, but a circuit is needed for every element, so power consumption and data volume become large. Between the two is the hybrid scheme, in which each of a small number of RF chains drives many elements in analog, and a digital stage combines the chains.

Combining the signals of N elements in phase improves the S/N N times on receive, because the signals add as voltages and uncorrelated noise adds as power (array gain). On transmit, the total power of the elements is N times larger and the array gain is also N times larger, so the EIRP grows in proportion to N². At millimeter waves the path loss is large, but the short wavelength allows many elements in a small area, and this array gain makes up for the loss, which is why beamforming is indispensable there. In exchange, the sharper the beam, the more it must search for and track the other station, so beam search and tracking procedures are also part of system design.

faq.q: How does beamforming differ from MIMO spatial multiplexing?
faq.a: Beamforming uses several elements to reinforce one signal in a particular direction and raise the S/N. Spatial multiplexing uses several antennas to send separate data streams at the same time and raise the data rate. Real systems combine the two.

faq.q: Does adding elements reduce the path loss itself?
faq.a: No. Path loss is set by distance and frequency. Adding elements raises the array gain, which increases the received power or S/N, so that much more loss can be tolerated.

faq.q: Is digital beamforming always the best scheme?
faq.a: It is the most flexible, but the per-element ADCs, DACs and processing make power consumption and cost high. In millimeter-wave equipment with many elements, hybrid or analog schemes are often chosen.

アレー利得.desc: The improvement in S/N over a single element when the element outputs are combined in phase. With uncorrelated noise it is N times (10 log₁₀ N dB) for N elements.

レイリーフェージング.desc: Fading when no direct wave arrives and only many scattered waves do. The envelope follows a Rayleigh distribution and the power an exponential distribution, with deep fades over about half a wavelength of movement.

about.p: Where there is no line-of-sight direct wave and many waves reflected and scattered by buildings and the ground arrive, the received signal is the sum of many waves with random phases. By the central limit theorem, its in-phase and quadrature components each follow a zero-mean normal distribution, the envelope √(I² + Q²) follows a Rayleigh distribution, and the power follows an exponential distribution. As the receiver moves, the phase relations among the waves change, so the received level fades deeply about every half wavelength of movement. Even without moving, the same fluctuation occurs if nearby vehicles or people move. It is the most basic fading model for mobile communication in urban areas.

Because the power is exponentially distributed, the probability of falling below x times the mean is 1 − e⁻ˣ, which is nearly x when x is small. The probability of being 10 dB below the mean is about 10%, 20 dB below about 1%, and 30 dB below about 0.1%: each additional 10 dB cuts it to 1/10. So keeping reception at 99% of times or places with a single antenna needs a margin of about 20 dB relative to the mean. The fades are short, and the faster the movement, the more frequent and shorter they become. This rate is set by the maximum Doppler frequency.

Making up for the depth of the fades with power is inefficient, so the basic countermeasure is diversity, which uses several received signals that fluctuate independently. Receiving with two antennas about half a wavelength apart or with antennas of different polarization, and then selecting or combining by maximal ratio combining, greatly lowers the probability of fading at the same time. In time, interleaving and error correction spread the effect of fades, and in frequency, OFDM does so by coding across a wide band. When a strong direct wave is present, the Rician fading model is used instead of Rayleigh.

faq.q: How do Rayleigh fading and Rician fading differ?
faq.a: Rayleigh is the case with no direct wave and only scattered waves; Rician is the case where scattered waves add to a strong direct wave. When the power ratio K of direct to scattered waves is 0, Rician matches Rayleigh.

faq.q: Why does the received level change over about half a wavelength of movement?
faq.a: When the receiving point moves half a wavelength, the path length of each wave changes by up to half a wavelength depending on its direction, so its phase changes by up to 180°. Waves that were reinforcing turn to cancelling, so the received level changes greatly.

faq.q: Are Rayleigh fading and shadowing the same thing?
faq.a: No. Rayleigh fading is the fast fluctuation over about a wavelength caused by multipath interference, while shadowing is the slow fluctuation over tens of meters or more caused by obstruction from buildings and the like.

ライスフェージング.desc: Fading when scattered waves add to a strong direct wave. The larger the K-factor, the power ratio of direct to scattered waves, the smaller the fluctuation; at K = 0 it becomes Rayleigh fading.

遅延スプレッド.desc: The spread of the delays of waves arriving by multipath, expressed as a power-weighted rms value. The larger it is, the narrower the coherence bandwidth and the more likely intersymbol interference becomes.

about.p: If a very short pulse is sent from the transmitter, waves with different path lengths arrive at the receiver with slightly different delays, giving a distribution of received power against delay (the delay profile). The delay spread expresses the spread of this distribution as the standard deviation (rms value) στ about the power-weighted mean delay. Note that it is not the maximum delay from the first to the last wave, but a spread in which stronger waves count more heavily. Values vary widely with the environment: tens of ns indoors, around 1 µs in urban areas, and several µs or more in places such as areas surrounded by mountains.

Seen in frequency, the spread of delays becomes ripple in the channel response. The larger the delay spread, the finer the spacing of the ripple, and the narrower the coherence bandwidth, the range of frequencies over which the channel can be regarded as nearly the same. As a guideline, with the definition at correlation 0.5, Bc ≈ 1/(5στ), about 200 kHz for στ = 1 µs. If the signal bandwidth is much narrower than this the fading is flat, and if it is wider the fading is frequency-selective, with notches in the band. The factor differs by definition, so use the same definition when comparing.

In the time domain, when the delay spread is not negligible compared with the symbol duration, delayed waves overlap the next symbol and cause intersymbol interference. In high-speed single-carrier transmission this must be removed with an equalizer. OFDM divides a wide band into many narrow subcarriers to lengthen each symbol, and also adds a cyclic prefix in front of each symbol to absorb the delayed waves. The cyclic prefix is chosen longer than the spread of delays expected in the environment. The spread of delays is also a source of frequency diversity, and coding across a wide band spreads the effect of fades.

faq.q: How does delay spread differ from maximum delay?
faq.a: The maximum delay is the time from the first wave to the last. The delay spread is the standard deviation of the delays weighted by the power of each wave, so weak delayed waves count for little.

faq.q: Is a large delay spread always bad for communication?
faq.a: It is a disadvantage in that intersymbol interference must be dealt with, but since the fades fall at different places at different frequencies, applying error correction over a wide band gives a frequency diversity effect.

faq.q: How long should the cyclic prefix of OFDM be?
faq.a: Longer than the spread of delayed waves expected in the environment. A longer prefix is more robust to delay, but it adds time in which no data is sent and lowers efficiency, so it is set by balancing the two.

コヒーレンス帯域幅.desc: The range of frequencies over which the channel's frequency response can be regarded as nearly the same. It is inversely proportional to the delay spread, and a signal band wider than it experiences frequency-selective fading.

コヒーレンス時間.desc: The length of time over which the state of the channel can be regarded as nearly the same. It is inversely proportional to the maximum Doppler frequency (Doppler spread) and is shorter for faster movement and higher frequency.

ダイバーシチ.desc: A technique that reduces deep fades by selecting or combining signals from several independently fluctuating branches (antennas, polarizations, frequencies, times and so on).

シャドウイング.desc: The change in the average received level over ranges of tens of meters or more caused by obstruction from buildings and terrain. Its dB value is treated as normally distributed (a log-normal distribution).

距離べき指数.desc: The value n that expresses to what power of distance the path loss is proportional. It is 2 in free space and 4 at long range in the two-ray model, and values of about 3 to 4 are common in urban areas and indoors.

スーパーヘテロダイン受信機.desc: A receiver that mixes the received signal with a local oscillator to convert it to a fixed intermediate frequency and selects the channel with a fixed IF filter. The image frequency must be removed ahead of the mixer.

ダイレクトコンバージョン受信機.desc: A receiver that sets the LO equal to the received frequency and converts directly to I and Q baseband. It is easy to integrate but is affected by DC offset, IQ imbalance and second-order distortion.

about.h: How it works and its advantages
about.p: A direct-conversion receiver tunes the local oscillator (LO) to the received frequency and uses two LOs 90° apart to convert the received signal directly to I and Q baseband. Because the IF is zero, it is also called a zero-IF receiver. It needs neither the external IF filter nor the image-rejection filter required by a superheterodyne, and channel selection can be done with baseband low-pass filters and digital processing, so it is easy to integrate on a CMOS chip and to adapt to multiple frequency bands.
