It is widely used in the receivers of mobile phones and wireless LANs.

Because the signal is converted to right around DC, unwanted components arising near DC become interference directly. LO leakage that reflects off the LNA input or the antenna and returns to the mixer mixes with the LO itself; this self-mixing produces a DC offset whose size changes with the surroundings of the antenna and the gain setting. In addition, the amplitude variation of a strong interferer, or the difference frequency of two interferers, appears near DC through the mixer's second-order distortion. DC offset calibration, AC coupling, and differential mixers with high IIP2 are therefore used. Low-frequency 1/f noise also degrades sensitivity, especially in CMOS circuits.

In zero-IF, the components on the upper and lower sides of the RF signal are converted to the positive and negative frequencies of the baseband. If the gain or phase of the I and Q paths differ, part of the +f component leaks into −f as a mirror image, and the signal interferes with itself. For small errors, the image rejection ratio can be estimated from the relative gain error ε and the phase error θ (in radians) as IRR ≈ 4/(ε² + θ²); a gain error of 2% alone gives about 40 dB, for example. In OFDM and high-order QAM this sets an upper limit on the EVM, so the errors are usually estimated from a known signal and corrected digitally.

faq.q: How do zero-IF and low-IF differ?
faq.a: Zero-IF converts the center of the channel to DC, while low-IF converts it to a low IF about the width of the channel. Low-IF avoids DC offset and 1/f noise more easily, but the adjacent channel becomes the image, so the image must be removed by I/Q signal processing.

faq.q: Why does the DC offset change over time?
faq.a: Because its main cause, self-mixing of LO leakage, changes with the reflections around the antenna and with the gain switched by the AGC. So in addition to a one-time calibration, processing that tracks and subtracts the DC shift during reception is also used.

faq.q: Are there direct-conversion transmitters too?
faq.a: Yes. Direct-conversion transmitters, which modulate the LO directly with I and Q baseband signals, are widely used. On the transmit side too, the image caused by IQ imbalance and carrier leakage caused by LO leakage are problems, and they are corrected by calibration.

Low-IF受信機.desc: A receiver that converts to a low intermediate frequency comparable to the channel bandwidth. It avoids DC offset and 1/f noise more easily, but the image, which falls in the adjacent channel, must be removed by I/Q signal processing.

イメージ除去比.desc: The ratio of the output powers of the wanted signal and the image when both are input at the same strength. It can be estimated from the I/Q gain error ε and phase error θ as IRR ≈ 4/(ε² + θ²).

IQ不平衡.desc: A mismatch in gain or phase between the orthogonal I and Q paths. In zero-IF, the mirror image of the signal falls on itself, degrading the image rejection ratio and EVM.

AGC.desc: Automatic gain control: the function that automatically varies a receiver's gain so that the level of the signal entering the ADC or demodulator stays nearly constant even as the input strength changes.

受信感度.desc: The minimum input power a receiver can demodulate at a specified quality. It is estimated as −174 dBm/Hz + 10 log₁₀B + noise figure + required S/N (dBm).

about.p: Receiver sensitivity is the minimum input power a receiver can demodulate at a specified quality (bit error rate, S/N, and so on). The input-referred noise power is the thermal noise power density at 290 K, −174 dBm/Hz, plus the bandwidth term 10 log₁₀B and the receiver noise figure NF; adding the S/N needed for demodulation gives the estimate sensitivity = −174 + 10 log₁₀B + NF + S/N (dBm). For example, with a 20 MHz bandwidth, an NF of 7 dB and a required S/N of 5 dB, it is about −89 dBm. The smaller (more negative) the value, the weaker the signals that can be received.

Each term of the formula is itself a means of improvement. The bandwidth is narrowed to the minimum the signal needs. The noise figure is set mostly by the noise figure and gain of the first-stage LNA and by the loss of filters and cables ahead of it, so a low-noise amplifier is placed close to the antenna. The required S/N can be reduced by lowering the modulation order or strengthening error correction. However, both narrowing the bandwidth and lowering the modulation order reduce the data rate, so sensitivity and transmission speed trade off against each other. The usual design order is to fix the required data rate first and then tighten the sensitivity with the remaining terms.

about.h: Sensitivity in the presence of interferers
about.p: Sensitivity is the value in a quiet environment with no interferers. In practice, a strong nearby interferer lowers the sensitivity by reducing the gain through compression of the LNA or mixer, or by increasing the in-band noise through reciprocal mixing with the local oscillator's phase noise (blocking, or desensitization). Third-order intermodulation distortion of two interferers can also fall in band. Radio standards therefore check, in addition to sensitivity in quiet conditions, whether the specified quality can be maintained with specified interferers applied, through tests such as blocking and adjacent channel selectivity.

faq.q: What is the −174 dBm/Hz in the sensitivity formula?
faq.a: It is the thermal noise power density at 290 K: kT = 1.38×10⁻²³ × 290 ≈ 4×10⁻²¹ W/Hz expressed in dBm. Receiver noise is found by starting from this and adding the bandwidth and noise figure.

faq.q: How are sensitivity and link margin related?
faq.a: The difference between the received power and the sensitivity is the link margin. With a received power of −80 dBm and a sensitivity of −89 dBm the margin is 9 dB, and communication can continue even if fading lowers the received power by that much.

faq.q: If the noise figure improves by 1 dB, how much does the sensitivity improve?
faq.a: With other conditions unchanged, the sensitivity also improves (gets smaller) by 1 dB, because the noise figure is added directly in the sensitivity formula.

量子化雑音.desc: The error that arises when an ADC rounds continuous values to discrete ones, treated as noise. The S/N of an ideal N-bit ADC with a full-scale sine wave is 6.02N + 1.76 dB.

整合回路.desc: A circuit that transforms a load impedance into a value that, seen from the source, gives no reflection or receives the maximum power. It is built from low-loss reactive elements or transmission lines.

L型整合回路.desc: A matching network using one series and one shunt reactance. The shunt element goes on the higher-resistance side, and the Q is fixed by the resistance ratio as √(Rhigh/Rlow − 1).

about.p: An L-network is the simplest matching network, using one series reactance and one shunt reactance. When matching resistances Rhigh and Rlow, the shunt element goes on the higher-resistance side and the series element on the lower-resistance side. This is because adding a series reactance to the smaller resistance lets its conductance, once converted to admittance, be brought down to 1/Rhigh, and the remaining susceptance can be canceled by the shunt element. Placed the other way round, the parallel combination only makes the resistance smaller, and no match is possible.

The circuit Q is Q = √(Rhigh/Rlow − 1), fixed by the resistance ratio. The series element's reactance is Xs = Q·Rlow and the shunt element's is Xp = Rhigh/Q. For 50 Ω and 10 Ω, for example, Q = 2, Xs = 20 Ω and Xp = 25 Ω; at 1 GHz the shunt capacitor is about 6.4 pF and the series inductor about 3.2 nH. The higher the Q, the narrower the bandwidth, so with a large resistance ratio a single L-section does not give enough bandwidth. In that case, a multisection L-network with an intermediate resistance √(Rhigh·Rlow) is used to lower the Q of each section.

For the same resistance ratio, a series inductor with a shunt capacitor gives a low-pass form, and a series capacitor with a shunt inductor gives a high-pass form. Both match at the design frequency, but the low-pass form reduces harmonics and so suits power amplifier outputs, while the high-pass form can block DC with its series capacitor. A transistor's parasitic capacitance and package inductance are taken in (absorbed) as part of the matching network's elements, and components with those amounts subtracted are fitted.

faq.q: Can the Q of an L-network be chosen freely?
faq.a: No. It has only two element values, so fixing the resistance ratio also fixes the Q. Use a π- or T-network for a higher Q, or a multisection L-network for a lower Q.

faq.q: On which side should the shunt element go?
faq.a: On the higher-resistance side. For matching 50 Ω and 10 Ω, the shunt element goes on the 50 Ω side and the series element on the 10 Ω side.

faq.q: What if the load has reactance?
faq.a: Either take the load's reactance in as part of the series element, or cancel it first and then design an L-network between resistances. With a Smith chart, both can be handled on the chart at the same time.

π型整合回路.desc: A three-element matching network of shunt, series and shunt elements. It can be viewed as two L-sections around a virtual resistance smaller than both terminations, letting Q be chosen separately from the resistance ratio.

T型整合回路.desc: A three-element matching network of series, shunt and series elements. It can be viewed as two L-sections around a virtual resistance larger than both terminations, and like the π-network it lets Q be chosen separately from the resistance ratio.

共役整合.desc: Making the load impedance the complex conjugate of the source impedance. The reactances cancel, and all of the source's available power can be drawn into the load.

about.p: The power that can be drawn into a load from a source with internal impedance Zs = Rs + jXs is maximized when the load is ZL = Zs* = Rs − jXs, the complex conjugate of the source. The reactances then cancel and the resistive parts are equal, and the source's available power |V|²/(8Rs) (where V is the amplitude of the open-circuit voltage) all goes to the load. If both source and load are pure resistances, conjugate matching simply means making the resistances equal. Even though the load power is maximized, the source's internal resistance dissipates the same power, so the efficiency is 50%.

about.h: How it differs from reflectionless matching
about.p: In transmission-line matching, the aim is to make the load equal to the characteristic impedance Z0 so there is no reflection. If Z0 is real and the source is also Z0, reflectionless matching and conjugate matching are the same condition. On the other hand, when the source impedance is complex, or for circuits with internal reactance such as transistors, the condition for drawing maximum power is expressed as a conjugate match. The role of a matching network is to make the actual load look like this conjugate value as seen from the source. Away from the design frequency the conjugate relation breaks down, so the match holds only within a certain bandwidth.

about.h: When conjugate matching is not optimal
about.p: Conjugate matching is the condition for maximum small-signal power (gain), but depending on the purpose it is not optimal. In a low-noise amplifier, the source impedance that minimizes the noise figure (Γopt) generally differs from the conjugate-match condition, and a compromise with noise matching is needed. In a power amplifier, the large-signal optimum load set by the limits of the output voltage and current swings differs from the conjugate value and is found by load-pull. Also, a simultaneous conjugate match of a transistor's input and output can be realized only when it is unconditionally stable.

faq.q: Does conjugate matching eliminate reflection?
faq.a: The reflection of power waves referenced to the source impedance disappears, but the reflection coefficient referenced to 50 Ω or another reference does not necessarily become zero. When the source is a pure resistance equal to the reference, the two coincide.

faq.q: What is the efficiency under conjugate matching?
faq.a: 50%, because the load and the source's internal resistance dissipate the same power. In circuits such as power supplies where high efficiency matters, the load resistance is made larger than the internal resistance.

faq.q: If the source is a pure 50 Ω resistance, what should the load be?
faq.a: A pure 50 Ω resistance. The complex conjugate of 50 Ω is 50 Ω, so the condition is the same as reflectionless matching.

雑音整合.desc: Setting an amplifier's source impedance to the value (Γopt) at which the noise figure reaches its minimum Fmin. It generally differs from conjugate matching, leaving some input reflection.

ボード・ファノの限界.desc: A relation showing that when a load containing reactance is matched with a lossless network, there is an upper limit on bandwidth and how small the reflection can be. For a parallel RC load, ∫ln(1/|Γ|)dω ≤ π/(RC).

等コンダクタンス円.desc: A circle on the Smith chart joining points of equal conductance. When a shunt element is added, the point moves along this circle.

サイクリックプレフィックス.desc: An interval formed by copying the end of an OFDM symbol and attaching it to the front. It absorbs delayed waves to prevent intersymbol interference and enables one-tap equalization per subcarrier.

about.p: In OFDM, part of the end of the useful symbol of length Tu produced by the IFFT is cut off and added to the front of the symbol before transmission. This added interval is the cyclic prefix (CP). At the receiver, the CP interval is discarded and only the remaining Tu interval is fed to the FFT. Waves delayed by multipath drag along the tail of the previous symbol, but if the delay is shorter than the CP, that tail falls within the CP interval and is discarded, so it does not overlap the demodulation of the next symbol. In broadcasting it is also called the guard interval.

Preventing intersymbol interference is not the CP's only effect. Seen from the interval taken into the FFT, the signal appears to continue periodically, so the linear convolution with the impulse response of the propagation path becomes the same as a circular convolution. After the FFT a circular convolution becomes a simple multiplication, so the received value on the k-th subcarrier takes the form H(k)X(k) plus noise. The receiver can equalize simply by dividing by the H(k) estimated for each subcarrier, which is far simpler than single-carrier schemes that need equalizers with many taps in the time domain.

about.h: Choosing the length and its cost
about.p: The CP is made longer than the delay spread of the expected environment (a value close to the maximum delay). A CP of length T can absorb path-length differences up to cT, about 1.4 km for 4.7 µs. On the other hand, the CP interval is discarded at the receiver, so the data rate falls by a factor of Tu/(Tu + Tcp), and the S/N also loses by the power in that interval. With a CP of 1/4 of the useful symbol duration, the efficiency is 80% and the S/N loss is about 1 dB. Narrowing the subcarrier spacing to lengthen Tu lowers the CP fraction, but then the system becomes more vulnerable to Doppler and frequency offset.

faq.q: Couldn't an interval with nothing sent (zeros) be used instead of the CP?
faq.a: A zero interval also prevents intersymbol interference, but the signal no longer appears circular over the FFT window, so the orthogonality between subcarriers breaks down. With a CP the convolution becomes circular and one-tap equalization can be used. Zero-padding schemes (ZP-OFDM) exist, but they need different processing at the receiver.

faq.q: Is a longer CP always better?
faq.a: It becomes more tolerant of delay, but the time that carries no data grows and the rate and S/N efficiency fall. The CP is made somewhat longer than the expected delay spread, and some schemes provide a separate long CP for environments with large delays.

faq.q: Does the CP also correct frequency offset?
faq.a: No. Frequency offset is a separate problem that breaks the orthogonality between subcarriers, and it is estimated and corrected using preambles and the like. The repeated structure of the CP is sometimes used for time synchronization and for estimating frequency offset.

サブキャリア.desc: Each of the individual carriers into which the band is divided in OFDM. The spacing is the reciprocal of the useful symbol duration and equals the sampling frequency divided by the number of FFT points.

パイロット信号.desc: A known signal sent for channel estimation and synchronization. In OFDM, pilots are placed sparsely on the time–frequency grid and the values in between are found by interpolation.

MIMO.desc: A radio scheme that uses multiple antennas at both the transmitter and the receiver. It can raise the rate by spatial multiplexing or raise reliability by diversity.

about.p: In MIMO with Nt transmit antennas and Nr receive antennas, the propagation path from each transmit antenna to each receive antenna is expressed as a complex gain, and these are arranged into an Nr-row, Nt-column channel matrix H that describes the whole. The received signal is y = Hx + n. Combined with OFDM, the propagation path becomes flat on each subcarrier, so this narrowband expression can be used as is on each subcarrier. In rich-scattering environments the elements of H vary independently, while with strong line of sight and closely spaced antennas the elements become highly correlated. The properties of this matrix determine the gain that can be obtained.

There are two broad ways to use MIMO. Spatial multiplexing sends different data from multiple antennas on the same frequency at the same time and separates them at the receiver; the number of streams is up to the rank of H, that is, min(Nt, Nr). Diversity sends the same data encoded with a space-time code or the like, and lowers the error rate by exploiting the Nt × Nr paths that fade independently. There is a trade-off between the two: the more the rate is raised, the less diversity is obtained, and schemes are switched according to the state of the propagation path.

At high S/N, MIMO channel capacity is roughly proportional to min(Nt, Nr) × log₂(S/N), so adding antennas increases capacity without widening the band. If the transmitter knows the channel matrix, singular value decomposition splits it into parallel channels without interference, and allocating power by water-filling maximizes capacity. If it does not, power is divided equally among the antennas and the receiver separates the streams by ZF, MMSE, maximum-likelihood detection and so on. The burden of feeding channel information back to the transmitter and errors in estimation also affect the capacity actually obtained.

faq.q: Does adding antennas raise the rate without limit?
faq.a: The number of streams is set by the smaller of the numbers of transmit and receive antennas, and the rank falls further if the propagation path is highly correlated. Adding antennas on only one side increases diversity or beamforming gain.

faq.q: How do MIMO and beamforming differ?
faq.a: Beamforming aligns one signal across multiple antennas to concentrate power, and can be seen as one way of using MIMO. Spatial multiplexing sends multiple streams over separate spatial paths.

faq.q: Is MIMO useless in line-of-sight environments?
faq.a: Antenna correlation becomes high and spatial multiplexing gain is hard to obtain, but beamforming gain is still available. Using two orthogonal polarizations often allows two streams to be sent even with line of sight.

空間多重.desc: In MIMO, a method of sending different data from multiple antennas on the same frequency at the same time and separating them at the receiver. The number of streams is up to min(Nt, Nr).

時空間ブロック符号.desc: A code that encodes symbols across multiple transmit antennas and multiple time instants to obtain transmit diversity without channel knowledge at the transmitter. The two-antenna version is the Alamouti code.

注水定理.desc: The result that when total power is divided among parallel channels, capacity is maximized by giving more to channels with lower noise/gain, so that each channel's noise/gain plus power reaches a common water level.

等価地球半径.desc: A representation of the bending of radio waves by atmospheric refraction in which the wave is a straight line and the earth's radius is multiplied by k. In a standard atmosphere k ≈ 4/3, about 8500 km.

about.p: The refractive index n of the atmosphere is slightly greater than 1, and because pressure, temperature and water vapor decrease with height, in a standard atmosphere it decreases by about 40×10⁻⁶ per km of height. When the refractive index is smaller higher up, the wave travels faster on its upper side, so its path bends gradually toward the side with the larger refractive index below, that is, toward the ground. The degree of bending is about 1/4 of the earth's curvature, so on line-of-sight links the wave follows the curve of the earth just slightly. As a result, the range of the radio wave extends a little beyond the geometric line of sight.

about.h: The idea of the k factor
about.p: Only the relative difference between the bending of the wave's path and the curvature of the earth matters for line of sight. So the wave is drawn as a straight line and, instead, the earth's radius is multiplied by k, giving a picture with the same difference. k = 1/(1 + R·dn/dh), and with R = 6370 km and dn/dh = −40×10⁻⁶ /km, k ≈ 4/3 and the effective earth radius is about 8500 km. In this picture, the distance from an antenna at height h to the horizon is √(2kRh), which for k = 4/3 is about 4.12√h km with h in m.

k changes with the weather. When the refractive index decreases gently, or increases with height, k < 1, the earth's bulge appears larger and the Fresnel zone is more easily obstructed by the ground or obstacles along the path. Conversely, when it decreases steeply k becomes larger; when dn/dh reaches −157×10⁻⁶ /km, k is infinite, and if it is steeper still a radio duct forms. In line-of-sight link design, antenna heights are chosen so that clearance remains even when k becomes small, and interference with distant stations is watched for when k becomes large.

faq.q: Can the value 4/3 be used anywhere?
faq.a: It is an average value for a standard mid-latitude atmosphere. It varies with region, season and time of day, and when checking link reliability, conditions with a smaller k (such as 2/3) are also examined.

faq.q: How much does using the effective earth radius extend the line-of-sight distance?
faq.a: The distance to the horizon is proportional to √k, so k = 4/3 gives about 1.15 times the distance for k = 1. For an antenna 100 m high, it extends from about 36 km to about 41 km.

faq.q: Is the optical line of sight the same as the radio line of sight?
faq.a: Not quite. The refractive index for visible light is hardly affected by water vapor, so the k for optical refraction is closer to 1 than for radio, and the radio line of sight reaches slightly farther.

ラジオダクト.desc: A phenomenon in a layer where the refractive index decreases steeply with height (dN/dh < −157 N/km), in which radio waves are trapped between the layer and the ground and reach far beyond the line of sight.

ナイフエッジ回折.desc: The bending of radio waves around the tip of a thin obstacle near the line of sight. The loss is set by the diffraction parameter v, and is about 6 dB when the tip touches the line of sight.

地表波.desc: A radio wave that travels along the surface of the earth. Vertically polarized, it reaches farther at lower frequencies and over the sea with its high conductivity. The main mode of medium-wave broadcasting.

臨界周波数.desc: The highest frequency at which a wave launched straight up into the ionosphere is reflected back. It is proportional to the square root of the layer's maximum electron density, about 9√N Hz (N in m⁻³).

MUF.desc: Maximum usable frequency. The highest frequency usable on an ionospheric-reflection path between two points; for a flat layer, the critical frequency divided by the cosine of the angle of incidence (secant law).

about.p: In the ionosphere, the refractive index becomes smaller as the electron density rises, and an obliquely entering wave is bent gradually and returns to the ground. The upper limit for a wave directed straight up to return is the critical frequency fc, and a wave whose angle of incidence measured from the layer's normal is θ returns up to the higher frequency fc/cos θ. This is the secant law; the more distant the station to be reached, the larger the angle of incidence and the higher the MUF. For example, with fc = 7 MHz and θ = 60°, the MUF is 14 MHz. In reality the curvature of the earth and ionosphere limits the angle of incidence, and the distance reached with one reflection from the F layer is up to about 4000 km.

about.h: Choosing between the MUF and the LUF
about.p: Waves above the MUF penetrate the layer and do not return. On the other hand, the lower the frequency, the larger the absorption in the daytime D layer, so there is a lowest frequency (the LUF) at which the strength needed for reception can be maintained. In shortwave communication, a frequency between this MUF and LUF is chosen. A frequency right at the MUF would penetrate with small fluctuations of the ionosphere, so the optimum working frequency (FOT) of about 85% of the MUF is used as a guideline. When the MUF falls and the LUF rises, the usable window narrows, and during sudden ionospheric disturbances accompanying solar flares the window may close altogether.

about.h: Varies with time and solar activity
about.p: The electron density of the ionosphere is produced by the sun's ultraviolet radiation, so the MUF is high in the day and low at night, and also changes greatly with season and with the roughly 11-year cycle of solar activity. In the daytime in years of high solar activity, the F-layer MUF exceeds 30 MHz, and long-distance communication is possible even in bands such as 28 MHz. At night the MUF falls, so operators switch to lower frequencies. The basic practice in shortwave operation is to change frequency according to the time of day, based on ionospheric observations and forecasts. The state of the ionosphere is observed with ionosondes, which send radio waves straight up while sweeping the frequency and measure the time for the reflection to return.

faq.q: What happens if a frequency above the MUF is used?
faq.a: The wave passes through the ionosphere into space and does not reach the distant station. This penetrating property is convenient for communicating with satellites.

faq.q: How do the critical frequency and the MUF differ?
faq.a: The critical frequency is the upper limit for return at vertical incidence and is a property of the layer itself. The MUF is the upper limit usable on a path joining two particular points, and the angle of incidence makes it higher than the critical frequency.

faq.q: Why do lower frequencies travel better at night?
faq.a: At night the D layer disappears and absorption decreases, while the electron density of the F layer falls and the MUF falls too. Higher frequencies penetrate more easily, and lower frequencies come to reach far.

秦の式.desc: An empirical path loss formula that expresses the urban measurements of Okumura and colleagues as equations. Within ranges such as 150–1500 MHz and 1–20 km, it gives the median loss.

比減衰.desc: Attenuation per km (dB/km) due to rain and the like. For rain it is written in the form γ = kR^α, with k and α set by frequency and polarization. Multiplying by the path length gives the attenuation.

低軌道.desc: A satellite orbit at altitudes of roughly a few hundred to 2000 km. The period is about 1.5 to 2 h, and propagation delay and loss are small, but many satellites and switching between them are needed.

about.p: By Kepler's third law, the period of a circular orbit is T = 2π√(a³/μ), where a is the orbital radius from the earth's center and μ is the earth's gravitational parameter, about 3.99×10¹⁴ m³/s². At an altitude of 550 km, a is about 6928 km, the period is about 96 min, and the satellite's speed √(μ/a) is about 7.6 km/s. The lower the orbit, the shorter the period and the higher the speed. Whereas the period of the geostationary orbit at about 36,000 km equals the earth's rotation period, a low earth orbit satellite circles the earth more than a dozen times a day and, seen from the ground, crosses the sky in a few minutes to about 20 minutes depending on altitude.

The distance to a low earth orbit satellite at the zenith is the altitude itself; at an altitude of 550 km it is about 1/65 of that to a geostationary satellite. The one-way propagation delay is only a few ms, much smaller than the roughly 0.24 s via a geostationary satellite, which suits communication needing quick interaction and response. Free-space path loss also falls with the square of the distance, and the ratio to a geostationary satellite exceeds 30 dB, so links can be made even with terminals with small antennas or little transmit power. At low elevation angles, however, the distance becomes several times longer, so the link is designed for the low-elevation condition.

The area one low earth orbit satellite can see is small, and the time it is visible from one point on the ground is limited, so continuous communication requires a constellation of many satellites arranged in several orbital planes. Terminals and ground stations switch communication to the next satellite before the current one sets below the horizon (handover). Satellites move quickly across the sky, so ground antennas track them either by turning mechanically or by steering the beam electronically with a phased array. With line-of-sight velocities of several km/s, it is also essential to predict Doppler shifts of up to tens of kHz from the orbit and correct for them.

faq.q: Why do low earth orbit satellites move faster than geostationary satellites?
faq.a: In a circular orbit gravity provides the centripetal force, so the speed is √(μ/a) and is higher closer to the earth: about 7.6 km/s at an altitude of 550 km and about 3.1 km/s in geostationary orbit.

faq.q: In low earth orbit, can one satellite provide communication?
faq.a: A satellite is visible for at most about 20 minutes per pass, so with one satellite communication is interrupted. Continuous service uses many satellites, switching from one to the next.

faq.q: Does low earth orbit have drawbacks?
faq.a: Challenges include the cost of launching and maintaining many satellites, the handover and tracking mechanisms, orbital decay due to atmospheric drag, and the disposal of satellites at the end of their service.

C/N₀.desc: The ratio of received carrier power to noise power per 1 Hz (noise power density). Its unit is dBHz, and it expresses link quality independent of bandwidth.

about.p: C/N is the ratio of carrier power C to the noise power N = kTB within the receiver bandwidth B. C/N₀, by contrast, is the ratio to the noise power density N₀ = kT before multiplying by bandwidth; it has the dimension of Hz and is written in dB as dBHz. The relation is C/N = C/N₀ − 10 log₁₀ B; for example, if C/N₀ is 80 dBHz and the bandwidth is 1 MHz (60 dBHz), C/N is 20 dB. C/N₀ allows the quality of the link itself to be compared before the receiver bandwidth is decided, so it is often used to evaluate satellite links and positioning receivers.

The received power is C = EIRP − L + G (dB) and the noise power density is N₀ = kT, so C/N₀ = EIRP − L + G/T − 10 log₁₀ k. Since 10 log₁₀ k = −228.6 dBW/(K·Hz), the last term is +228.6 dB. For example, with an EIRP of 50 dBW, a loss of 206 dB and a G/T of 20 dB/K, C/N₀ = 92.6 dBHz. L includes, besides free-space path loss, losses from the atmosphere and rain and losses from polarization and pointing errors. The transmitting side's performance is gathered in EIRP and the receiving side's in G/T, giving a clear picture of the link.

On digital links, the ratio of energy per bit Eb to N₀ determines the error rate. Since Eb = C/R (R is the bit rate), Eb/N₀ = C/N₀ − 10 log₁₀ R. With C/N₀ of 92.6 dBHz at 10 Mb/s (70 dB), Eb/N₀ is 22.6 dB, and the difference from the Eb/N₀ required by the modulation and coding is the link margin. Doubling the bit rate at the same C/N₀ lowers Eb/N₀ by 3 dB, so C/N₀ also serves as a guide for estimating the upper limit of the information rate that can be sent.

faq.q: What kind of unit is dBHz?
faq.a: C/N₀ is the ratio of a power to a power per 1 Hz, so it has the dimension of Hz. That value expressed in dB with 10 log₁₀ is dBHz.

faq.q: If C/N₀ is known, how is C/N found?
faq.a: With B the receiver's noise bandwidth, C/N = C/N₀ − 10 log₁₀ B (dB). The wider the bandwidth, the more noise enters and the lower C/N becomes.

faq.q: How are the uplink and downlink C/N₀ combined?
faq.a: With a transparent repeater the noise adds as linear values, so 1/(C/N₀)total = 1/(C/N₀)up + 1/(C/N₀)down. The result is even worse than the worse of the two links.

トランスポンダ.desc: The repeater carried on a communications satellite. It receives and amplifies the uplink signal, converts it to the downlink frequency and sends it back. There are also regenerative types that demodulate and remodulate.

スラントレンジ.desc: The oblique distance from an earth station to a satellite. It is longer at lower elevation angles, so propagation loss and delay are greatest under low-elevation conditions.

交差偏波識別度.desc: The ratio of the wanted-polarization component of a received signal to the component leaked into the orthogonal polarization. It expresses the separation on dual-polarized links and degrades with rain and other causes.

ファラデー回転.desc: The rotation of the orientation of linear polarization passing through the ionosphere, caused by the geomagnetic field and electrons. The rotation angle is inversely proportional to the square of frequency and is large at low frequencies.

指向損失.desc: The drop in gain when the center of an antenna's beam is off the direction of the other end. It is larger for large antennas with narrow beamwidths and at higher frequencies.

相互インダクタンス.desc: The quantity M expressing how much voltage a change of current in one coil induces in another coil. V₂ = jωMI₁, and it is set by the shape and arrangement of the coils.

結合係数.desc: The strength of the magnetic linkage between two coils, k = M/√(L₁L₂). It takes values from 0 to 1 and is set by the shape, distance and misalignment of the coils.

about.p: The coupling coefficient k is the mutual inductance M divided by the geometric mean of the two coils' self-inductances, k = M/√(L₁L₂). It can be thought of as the fraction of the flux produced by one coil that links the other, and it takes values between 0 and 1. In a transformer with two windings on an iron core it can exceed 0.99, but for coils separated by space it is small, about 0.01 to 0.3 in wireless power transfer, and in RFID, where the distance between card and reader changes, it varies even more.

The field on the axis of a circular coil of radius a is inversely proportional to d³ when the distance d is much larger than a, so k for two separated coils also falls sharply, in inverse proportion to d³. Doubling the distance makes k about 1/8. Up to a distance comparable to the coil radius, k is maintained to some extent, so the range of magnetically coupled power transfer can be said to be set by the size of the coils. Lateral misalignment and tilt between the coil planes also lower k, and depending on the misalignment the flux can cancel so that k approaches 0.

about.h: k does not change with resonance
about.p: k is a geometric quantity set by the shape, size and arrangement of the coils, and it does not change with frequency or with whether the coils are resonated with capacitors. Resonant wireless power transfer achieves higher efficiency at a distance not because k increases but because high coil Q makes k√(Q₁Q₂), which sets the upper limit of efficiency, large. On the other hand, if k is too large, frequency splitting occurs, in which the two coupled resonances separate, and the power that can be sent at the design frequency can actually fall.

faq.q: Why does k not reach 1?
faq.a: Part of the flux produced by one coil returns without passing through the other coil as leakage flux. For coils separated by space, the leakage is much larger.

faq.q: How can k be increased?
faq.a: Methods include making the coils larger, shortening the distance, aligning the axes, and providing a path for the flux with ferrite. Making the receiving coil extremely small compared with the transmitting coil lowers k.

faq.q: Is wireless power transfer impossible when k is small?
faq.a: No. The upper limit of efficiency is set by k√(Q₁Q₂), so by resonating high-Q coils, high efficiency can be obtained even with k of about 0.1.

ワイヤレス給電.desc: Technology for sending power without connecting wires. At short range it uses magnetic coupling between coils (inductive coupling, magnetic resonance coupling), and at long range radio waves such as microwaves.

kQ積.desc: k√(Q₁Q₂), combining the coupling coefficient k and the Q of the two coils. The upper limit of efficiency for power transfer between two resonant coils is determined by this value alone.

about.p: When power is sent between two resonant coils, the upper limit of efficiency with the load optimized is expressed using U = k√(Q₁Q₂) as ηmax = U²/(1 + √(1 + U²))². It is about 17% for U = 1, about 52% for 3, about 82% for 10 and about 98% for 100. When U is large, ηmax ≈ 1 − 2/U, and the fraction lost is inversely proportional to U. Frequency and coil size affect the efficiency limit only through U, which makes it one index for comparing designs.

about.h: Making up for weak coupling with Q
about.p: Even when k becomes small at a greater distance, high-Q coils keep U large. For example, even with k = 0.05, two coils with a Q of 200 give U = 10, for an efficiency limit of about 82%. This is why resonant wireless power transfer (magnetic resonance coupling) reaches distances comparable to the coil size. Raising Q means lowering the AC resistance of the winding (Litz wire or thick conductors) and avoiding losses in nearby metals and dielectrics. However, high Q narrows the resonance bandwidth and makes the system sensitive to resonant-frequency shifts from component variation and nearby objects, so frequency tuning or tracking becomes necessary.

The limiting efficiency is obtained when the receiving-side load resistance is RL = R₂√(1 + U²) (R₂ is the loss resistance of the receiving coil). The larger U, the much larger the optimum load becomes than the coil's loss resistance. Real loads are batteries and rectifier circuits whose value changes with the state of charge, so a DC-DC converter is placed on the receiving side or the transmitting-side voltage or frequency is adjusted to keep the equivalent load near the optimum value. Note also that the load giving maximum power and the load giving maximum efficiency generally do not coincide.

faq.q: If the kQ product is large, can power be sent any distance?
faq.a: In principle, the larger U, the higher the efficiency, but k falls sharply with the cube of distance, so with realistic Q values a few times the coil size is a rough guide.

faq.q: Is higher Q always better?
faq.a: The efficiency limit rises, but the bandwidth narrows and the system becomes sensitive to shifts in resonant frequency. Q is chosen by balancing this against how easily the system can follow changes in load and position.

faq.q: What is the efficiency when U = 1?
faq.a: ηmax = 1/(1 + √2)² ≈ 0.17, or about 17%. U of 10 gives about 82%, and exceeding 90% requires U of about 20 or more.

近傍界.desc: The field in the region sufficiently closer than λ/(2π) to an antenna or coil. Energy is mainly stored and flows back and forth, and the field weakens sharply with distance.

周波数分裂.desc: The phenomenon in which two resonant circuits at the same frequency, coupled more strongly than critical coupling, have their resonance split into two frequencies, f₀/√(1 ± k).

NFC.desc: A scheme that communicates over distances of a few cm using magnetic coupling at 13.56 MHz. Based on HF-band RFID technology, it is used for reading cards and similar tasks.

負荷変調.desc: A method in which a tag returns data by switching the load on its coil, changing the impedance seen from the reader through magnetic coupling.

HEMT.desc: A FET whose channel is the two-dimensional electron gas formed at a heterojunction interface. Its electron mobility and velocity are high; GaAs-based HEMTs are used for low noise and millimeter waves, GaN-based ones for high power.

about.h: A two-dimensional electron gas as the channel
about.p: A HEMT is a FET that joins two semiconductors with different bandgaps and uses as its channel the electrons confined in the narrow well at their interface (the two-dimensional electron gas, 2DEG). In GaAs-based devices, modulation doping, with donors only on the AlGaAs side, drops electrons into an InGaAs or GaAs channel and keeps them away from ionized impurities, reducing scattering. In AlGaN/GaN, crystal polarization gathers a high density of electrons at the interface even without doping. In both, the mobility and velocity are higher than in a MESFET with a doped channel, giving gain and low noise at high frequencies.

pHEMTs, with an InGaAs channel on a GaAs substrate, have a low noise figure and have been used in LNAs for satellite broadcast reception, handset switches and millimeter-wave amplifiers. HEMTs on InP substrates have even faster electrons and are used in circuits well above 100 GHz and in cryogenically cooled radio-astronomy receivers. GaN HEMTs have a high breakdown field and can be operated at drain voltages of 28–50 V, so their output power per gate width is several times that of GaAs or more, and they are used in power amplifiers for base stations, radar and satellite transmitters. They are often built on SiC substrates with high thermal conductivity, and lower-cost devices on Si substrates also exist.

An AlGaN/GaN HEMT is a normally-on device that has electrons in the channel even at zero gate voltage, and a negative gate voltage is needed to turn it off. Applying power in the wrong order can let a large current flow into the drain, so the bias sequence must be managed, for example by applying the negative gate voltage first. Challenges for GaN HEMTs include current collapse caused by traps and degradation from high fields and channel temperature, which are countered with surface passivation, field plates and thermal design that lowers the channel temperature. Lifetime depends strongly on channel temperature, so observing the maximum channel temperature in the datasheet is fundamental.

faq.q: What is the difference between a HEMT and a MESFET?
faq.a: Both are FETs with a Schottky gate, but a MESFET uses a doped layer as its channel while a HEMT uses the 2DEG at a heterojunction interface. A HEMT has less impurity scattering, so its electrons are faster and its noise is lower.

faq.q: What does the "p" in pHEMT mean?
faq.a: It stands for pseudomorphic. A lattice-mismatched InGaAs channel is made thin enough for the mismatch to be absorbed as strain, so it grows without dislocations.

faq.q: Can GaN HEMTs also be used in low-noise amplifiers?
faq.a: Yes. Their noise figure is often somewhat higher than that of GaAs pHEMTs, but they withstand strong inputs, so they are used in receivers where a protective limiter is to be omitted.

2次元電子ガス.desc: A layer of electrons confined in a thin well at a heterojunction interface that can move only in the plane. In AlGaN/GaN, polarization forms about 10¹³ cm⁻² of it without doping.

トランジション周波数.desc: The frequency fT at which the current gain |h21| with the output shorted falls to 1. For a FET, fT ≈ gm/(2π(Cgs + Cgd)); it is the basic measure of speed.

about.h: Definition and how it is found
about.p: The transition frequency fT is the frequency at which the current gain |h21| of a transistor with its output AC-shorted falls to 1 (0 dB). At high frequencies |h21| falls roughly in inverse proportion to frequency, at −20 dB/decade, so it is common to measure |h21| at a lower frequency within the instrument's range and extrapolate the line to 0 dB. For example, if |h21| is 20 dB (10 times) at 10 GHz, fT is about 100 GHz. S-parameters are measured and converted to h21, and the parasitics of the measurement setup are removed before extrapolating.

For a FET, fT ≈ gm/(2π(Cgs + Cgd)), so the larger the transconductance gm and the smaller the gate capacitance, the higher it is. Physically it can also be written as fT ≈ 1/(2πτ) using the time τ for electrons to cross under the gate, so it rises as the gate length Lg is shortened and the electron velocity v is raised (τ ≈ Lg/v). HEMTs are fast because their electron velocity is high, and fine-geometry CMOS reaches hundreds of GHz because its gate length is short. In bipolar transistors, it is set by the sum of the base transit time and the charging times of the emitter and collector junctions.

Whereas fT is set by current gain, the maximum oscillation frequency fmax is the frequency at which the power gain with optimum input and output matching falls to 1. fmax depends on parasitic elements such as the gate resistance, output conductance and feedback capacitance, so for the same fT, fmax varies greatly with the structure and can be either higher or lower than fT. As a guide to the upper frequency limit for building amplifiers and oscillators, fmax has the more direct meaning, and practical circuits are often designed at a fraction of it.

faq.q: If fT is 100 GHz, can a 100 GHz amplifier be built?
faq.a: At fT the current gain is exactly 1, so no practical gain is obtained. Whether amplification is possible is determined by fmax, and to get enough gain a device with fmax several times higher than the operating frequency is chosen.

faq.q: Does fT change with bias?
faq.a: Yes. gm and the capacitances change with current and voltage, so fT peaks at a certain current. The fT in a datasheet is usually the value under the conditions that give the highest value.

faq.q: Are ft and Ft the same thing?
faq.a: They refer to the same quantity, but writing fT with a capital T subscript is the usual convention. T is the initial of transition.

最大発振周波数.desc: The frequency fmax at which a transistor's maximum available power gain (or unilateral power gain) falls to 1. Set by gate resistance and feedback capacitance, it is a guide to the upper limit for amplification and oscillation.

電流コラプス.desc: A phenomenon in GaN HEMTs in which, after a high drain voltage is applied, electrons are captured by traps at the surface or in the buffer, raising the on-resistance and temporarily reducing the current.

HBT.desc: A bipolar transistor whose emitter uses a material with a wider bandgap than the base. SiGe HBTs can be made in Si processes, and GaAs HBTs are used in handset power amplifiers.

LDMOS.desc: A lateral high-voltage MOSFET made in Si. A drift region on the drain side raises its breakdown voltage so it operates at 28–50 V, and it is used in power amplifiers for base stations and broadcasting below a few GHz.

バラクタダイオード.desc: A diode that uses the change in depletion-layer capacitance with reverse bias voltage. It is used for tuning VCO frequency and in voltage-tuned filters.

位相周波数比較器.desc: A circuit that compares the edges of the reference and the divided VCO signal and outputs the phase and frequency difference as the widths of UP and DN pulses. It is used together with a charge pump.

チャージポンプ.desc: A circuit that sources or sinks a constant current only during the PFD's UP and DN pulses, delivering charge to the loop filter. Current mismatch and leakage cause reference spurs.

ループフィルタ.desc: The low-pass filter that converts the charge-pump current into the VCO control voltage. A series RC creates a zero that secures phase margin, and it sets the loop bandwidth.

ループ帯域.desc: The range over which a PLL can track, set near the frequency where the open-loop gain is 1. Inside it the reference-side noise, and outside it the VCO noise, appears at the output.

about.p: The loop bandwidth of a PLL is the frequency range over which the loop can follow phase changes, set near the frequency where the open-loop gain is 1 (the crossover frequency). In a charge-pump PLL, the open-loop gain is set by the product of the charge-pump current, the loop-filter impedance and the VCO sensitivity, divided by the division ratio N. Placing the loop-filter zero and pole on either side of the crossover maximizes the phase margin, which is often chosen to be around 45–60°. The loop bandwidth changes when N changes, so synthesizers covering a wide range switch the charge-pump current to maintain it.

The loop acts as a low-pass filter for the noise of the reference, phase detector, charge pump and divider, and as a high-pass filter for VCO noise. Inside the loop bandwidth, therefore, the reference-side noise appears at the output multiplied by 20 log₁₀ N, and outside it the VCO's own noise appears. When the integrated phase noise (jitter) is to be minimized, a guide is to place the loop bandwidth near the offset where the two noises, referred to the output, cross. The larger the VCO noise, the more a wider bandwidth pays off.

The narrower the loop bandwidth, the more strongly the loop filter attenuates comparison-frequency components and fractional-N quantization noise, so spurs and far-offset noise become smaller. On the other hand, the lock time after a frequency switch lengthens roughly in inverse proportion to the loop bandwidth. In addition, because comparisons in the loop take place discretely, bringing the loop bandwidth close to the comparison frequency impairs stability, so the bandwidth is usually kept to between a few tens of times and about 10 times below the comparison frequency. Fast lock, which widens the bandwidth only during a switch, is a technique that reconciles this trade-off.

faq.q: Is the loop bandwidth the same as the closed-loop 3 dB bandwidth?
faq.a: They are close but not the same. Designs often express it as the frequency where the open-loop gain is 1, and the closed-loop 3 dB bandwidth is about 1 to 2 times that, depending on the phase margin.

faq.q: What happens to lock time when the loop bandwidth is widened?
faq.a: It shortens roughly in inverse proportion to the bandwidth. However, reference-spur attenuation decreases, and the in-band reference-side noise also appears over a wider range.

faq.q: How is the optimum loop bandwidth chosen?
faq.a: Refer the reference-side noise and the VCO noise to the output, overlay them, and use as a guide the bandwidth that minimizes the integrated phase noise. Then adjust it to meet the spur and lock-time requirements.

フラクショナルN PLL.desc: A PLL that switches its division ratio over time so that the average is a fraction. It can tune the output in fine steps while keeping a high comparison frequency, but needs countermeasures against spurs from the switching.

about.h: How a fractional division ratio is made
about.p: In an integer-N PLL, the output step equals the comparison frequency, so fine steps require a low comparison frequency and a large division ratio. A fractional-N PLL switches the division ratio over time, for example between N and N + 1, making the average division ratio N + F, where F is the fractional part. For example, with a comparison frequency of 50 MHz, N = 49 and F = 0.004, the output is 2450.2 MHz. The comparison frequency can be kept high, so the division ratio is smaller, the multiplication of in-band phase noise is reduced, and the loop bandwidth can be widened for faster switching.

about.h: Turning the error into noise with ΔΣ modulation
about.p: Switching the division ratio with a simple period makes the phase error repeat with a period set by the fractional part, producing large fractional spurs. Most devices therefore generate the sequence of division ratios with a ΔΣ modulator. The ΔΣ modulator turns the switching error into noise that is small at low offsets and larger at high offsets (noise shaping), which the loop's low-pass characteristic then removes. Higher-order ΔΣ makes the far-offset noise rise steeply, so the loop-filter order is raised to suppress it. If the phase detector or charge pump is nonlinear, high-frequency noise folds down to low offsets, so ensuring linearity is important.

A problem specific to fractional-N is the integer-boundary spur, which appears when the output is very close to an integer multiple of the comparison frequency. The VCO output and harmonics of the comparison frequency mix inside the circuit, and a spur forms at their difference frequency, that is, at an offset of fractional part × comparison frequency. When the offset is smaller than the loop bandwidth, the loop does not attenuate it, which makes it especially troublesome. Countermeasures include changing the comparison frequency to move the output away from integer multiples and reducing coupling between the reference path and the output path.

faq.q: Is fractional-N always better than integer-N?
faq.a: It has advantages in in-band noise and switching speed, but it adds fractional spurs, integer-boundary spurs and ΔΣ noise. In applications where coarse steps are acceptable, integer-N can be better in terms of spurs.

faq.q: How fine can the output step be made?
faq.a: It is set by the number of bits in the accumulator that determines the fractional part, giving a resolution of the comparison frequency divided by, for example, 2 to the 24th power. Steps finer than 1 Hz are possible.

faq.q: How is the ΔΣ order chosen?
faq.a: A higher order reduces low-offset noise and spurs but increases far-offset noise. Third order is common, and the loop filter attenuates with an order at least as high.

ΔΣ変調.desc: A method that feeds back the quantization error, turning it into noise that is small at low frequencies and larger at high frequencies (noise shaping). It is used in ΔΣ ADCs and fractional-N PLLs.

ジッタ.desc: The fluctuation of a signal's edge times before and after their ideal positions. For oscillators, the phase noise is integrated over a range of offsets and converted to time with σt = σφ/(2πf₀).

ロック時間.desc: The time from switching a PLL's frequency until the output frequency or phase settles within the allowed error. It is roughly inversely proportional to the loop bandwidth.
